Statement of superannuation and retiring allowances in the Civil Service from January 1, 1920, to December 31, 1920.-Sir Henry Drayton.
Fifty-third Annual Report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.-Hon. C. C. Ballantyne.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. James Mclsaac for an address to His Excellency the Governor General, in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, resumed from Wednesday, February 16.

Mr. Speaker, I
must first thank the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who, in the temporary absence from the Chamber yesterday of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), was leading the House between half past five and six o'clock, for his kindness in calling it six o'clock when it was only 5.45, in order that I might have a better opportunity of connected discourse.
I think it must have struck the members of this House and the people of this country that no serious attempt has so far been made by speakers on your right, Sir, to advance any argument against the amendment to the Address proposed by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. King). We had yesterday, as I have already said, a most interesting and inspiring address upon the League of Nations, but really no attempt was made to answer the resolution which preceded from this side of the House. So I am therefore driven back to discuss the remarks made by the Prime Minister, and this to the best of my poor ability I shall endeavour to do.

The Prime Minister takes this position. He says:	This House was elected by a
majority of the electors some few years ago; we have a majority in the House, and as long as we have a majority in the House, elected by a majority of the constituencies in this country, I propose to carry on. That, as I understand it, is the constitutional position which he takes. Now, first of all, this vote will show, and not until the votes are counted will it be demonstrated whether the Prime Minister has a majority of the votes in this House. That is something yet to be ascertained.
Secondly, has the Prime Minister a majority of the votes in this country? Why, just before the last election there was an Election Act passed for the purpose of disfranchising all those who might be suspected of political tendencies against the Prime Minister and his party, and of doubling up all those votes that would likely be in their favour. Soldiers' wives, soldiers' mothers and soldiers' sisters were all given the vote to the exclusion of other people just as deserving, and I remember in my riding noting with some amusement that soldiers' sweethearts were not given the vote, because although a soldier under our law can have only one wife he might have, and often had, many sweethearts. But that, after all, although important, is not as important an another point which I propose to prove before the House, and which I believe will be accepted by all .unbiassed minds, whether in the Chamber or outside of it.
The proposition which I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, is this:	That there was
at the time of the last general election an undertaking made by and on behalf of the Government that it would, if returned to power, only hold office for the time of the war and during demobilization. There was ' the agreement made, and I propose to prove it out of the mouths of ministers of the Crown at that time. Hon. Mr. Carvell, who now occupies the position of chairman of the Railway Board, was a Unionist minister from the province of New Brunswick. During the course of one of the sessions of 1919 the question of the formation of the Union Government came up, and this is what Mr. Carvell said:
I can only say that when I entered this Government-I am not going- over the very, very long and somewhat unpleasant conditions which existed between the month of April and October 1917, possibly another occasion may arise when they can be discussed-I did so after the most mature deliberation, which many of my good old friends know all about, and nobody
5i
knows so well as does my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's-I did so for one specific purpose and for a specified time. The purpose I am happy to say, has been achieved! The time has not yet expired. During the election in the Province of New Brunswick 1 issued a letter to my constituents and to the people of our Province setting forth the fact that the Government was to be of an equal number of former Conservatives and former Liberals, for the purpose of carrying on the war and finding recruits for our army, and that it would continue for the duration of the war and a reasonable time thereafter for demobilization. Demobilization has not yet been completed, and so far as I am concerned my contract has not expired.
Just as soon as demobilization was completed Mr. Carvell resigned from the Government because he regarded his contract as having expired.
What followed when his contract was terminated?

He was given the high quasi-judicial office of chairman of the Railway Commission, and his appointment to that office emphasizes the value of the citation which I have just made. Now, we have such a thing in this country as ministerial responsibility, and that responsibility is a joint one. When a minister of the Crown makes a declaration on a question of high importance such as was the question mentioned in this letter, he binds not only himself but his colleagues as well. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) was one of the colleagues of Mr. Carvell when he made that statement, and he was bound thereby. That is the statement of the present Prime Minister as well as of Mr. Carvell, and it was a direct undertaking of the present Prime Minister that this Government-he says that the present Government is a continuation of the last; that is his contention-would, as soon as demobilization was over, cease to exist, and an appeal would, of course as a matter of consequence, be made to the people. There were others who spoke in the same language. I quote from a speech of the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) delivered at Winnipeg on October 27, 1917. Said he:
I have not sacrificed' my liberalism. My liberal principles are part of myself and will stay with me until I die. But this is not the time to quarrel over political view-points on domestic issues. The whole issue, the sole reason for the union of parties is to win the war.
Before I go further I wish to protest, as I have protested before in this House and elsewhere, against the assumption that there was any difference in the desire to win the war between people who were

Liberals and those who were Conservatives at the time of the last election. We differed as to methods but not as to aim and object. And the oft-repeated assertion, repeated at that time and, I am sorry to say, even since, that it was a question between the Union Government, to win the war, and the Liberals, to abandon the boys in the trenches, was one of the most ungenerous and wicked perversions of the truth ever perpetrated by a political party for their own political ends. Its ungenerousness was shown by the fact that among the Liberal leaders of the day was the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), who was languishing in a German prison. Besides that, the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), Mr. Graham, Mr. Oliver, all had boys at the front who then or shortly after were to fill the graves of heroes who had died for their country. The sons of our friend the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and of Mr. E. M. McDonald, as well as those of many other Liberals, were fighting in the trenches then. The member for Maisonneuve suffered the loss of his only boy. But still we were taunted at that time that we were not in favour of winning the war. How. wicked was that statement is shown also in the fact that it divided race from race, province from province, religion from religion. I remember some sessions ago that the hon. gentleman who now occupies the high position of Prime Minister, stated on the floor of the , House, when the Liberals were laughing at some unconsciously amusing thing he had said, that our interest in the war was measured by our laughter. I protested then, and I protest to-day when he says that the great issue was one of winning the war. We differed in regard to methods, it is true, but I would not have this House forget that the method proposed was one of selective conscription, and that after this method had been put into force, only a few months had elapsed before the same Mr. Carvell, one of the leading members of the Government at that time, said that by a round-about, clumsy method they had been able to secure only 30,000 men.
Now, after this digression, made necessary by the repetition of what I regard as an unvenerable falsehood, I return to my argument as to the understanding between the parties. I quote again from that former champion of Western Liberalism, the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization. He spoke at Vancouver on

the 31st of October, and in the Vancouver Sun he is reported as having said:
I'm for plain speaking, and I intend so to speak. I am a Liberal, and when all is over I intend to remain a Liberal, because I believe in Liberal principles. I have been fighting- Toryism all my life, and I propose after the war to take up that fight just where I left off.
We have heard of the warrior taking his rest with his martial cloak around him. It is about time that this warrior of Western Liberalism took off his cloak, and began to fight. But so far we have not seen any symptoms of his entering upon the engagement. But not only were these statements made by those men high in the councils of the Unionist party, but the people so understood. Let me read to you, Mr. Speaker, the undertaking which was signed by those members of the primaries in Vancouver, who were voting for delegates to the Unionist Convention and who nominated one of my friends at whom I am now looking, the member for one of the seats of Vancouver City:
I, tile undersigned, do hereby pled'ge my support and influence to the present Unionist Government and the policy enunciated by them, i. e., the immediate and continuous enforcement of the Military Service Act, 1917, the mobilization of all our resources, the taxation of wealth, and the prevention of profiteering, and I agree to support the candidate selected at the Convention.
That was the view expressed by people connected with the formation of the Union* Government; they were the views held by supporters of the Union Government in British Columbia. Now, let us proceed to another province, and again let us quote from the words of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization. He is reported in the Regina Leader of Dec. 17 as saying:
Keferring to his own position, Mr. dalder said that it had been suggested that he had been duped by the Tories and that he would stand as a cipher when he got down to Ottawa.
I want to tell you, he said, that Calder has not been duped by the Tories. I have never stood in the position of a cipher, and I do not propose to do so now. I have a very clear conception of what I am going into the Union Government for, and what I am going to do. With reference to the suggestion that it was still the same old Borden Governement and the Government of the big interests, Mr. Calder asked his audience whether they thought it could be the same Government with F. B. Carvell in it and with Mr. Maclean as a member, and whether it could be the same Government which included Alexander Crerar and General Mewburn; and I want to tell you that you don't know Mewburn yet. He is a fine fellow.
Hear, hear.

It is a matter of interest, Mr. Speaker, to know that the member for East Hamilton, so happily characterized in that paragraph, has left the Union Government; that the member for Marquette has left the Union Government; that Mr. Carvell has left the Union Government; I am not sure whether Mr. A. K. Maclean has yet resumed his seat on our side, I know his seat is here and waiting for him. An hon. gentleman beside me states he is going to be here.
Now I know it is somewhat tiresome when a lawyer cites evidence-
Hear, hear.

I do not, Mr. Speaker, expect the gentlemen sitting to your right to enjoy the reading of that evidence. As a matter of fact I am not speaking for their pleasure, but I trust for the country's profit.
Hear, hear.
Sir Thomas White, speaking at Brockville, said-
Order.
He is the member for Leeds.

No, I understand he is not the member for Leeds. I understand he has accepted an oifice of emolument, and I am perfectly in order when I refer to him, with all the dignity that should be attached to a knight, as Sir Thomas White.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must refer to him as the member for Leeds, and I hope he will adhere to the well-established rule in that regard with respect to every hon. gentleman.

I understand that I am not allowed to discuss the Speaker's ruling. His Honour will admit that I am one of the most obedient of the flock over which he presides, but he will allow me to state that the constitutional authorities differ somewhat from the view which he takes. However, the gentleman who occupied some time ago the position of member for Leeds, and whose occupancy of that position is now a matter of dispute and discussion, said on the 17th November, 1917:
Union Government is an accomplished fact today. It was born of the will of the Canadian people, the majority of whom have long and earnestly desired that party strife should cease, that National Government should be formed for the period of the war.
The Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie), speaking at Guelph on the 2nd October, 1917, said:
I believe in an union at the present time of all political forces for the prosecution of the war, irrespective of all political parties. In the past I have been looked upon as a strong party man but since May last I have publicly and' privately advocated a cessation of party strife, and I intend to continue in this course until the end of the war. It must not, however, be supposed that by pursuing this course that I have changed my Liberal principles, I have not done so.
The war is still on.

Again, there was a meeting of Conscriptionist Liberals held in Hamilton, Ontario, on November 2, 1917, where the following motion was passed:
That whereas, since the notice calling this convention was sent out a Union Government has been formed in which Liberals throughout the Dominion have joined this convention recording its belief that the formation of a Union Government for the duration of the war was highly desirable and in the best interests of ' Canada, and believing that thereby the share of Canada in the conduct of the present world war will be best served and the Government of the country most effectively and satisfactorily carried on during the period1 of the war, expresses its approval of the action of the Liberal members of the present Union Government in entering the same.
I do not think I should have to labour the point any more. It is absolutely true that the Liberals-and there were a certain number, a large number-who supported Union Government in 1917, did so under the direct promise, under the direct statement, that they were supporting a government for the duration of the war. I would not give any narrow or technical interpretation to these words "during the duration of the war." I would be prepared to extend that to cover demobilization. To be perfectly fair I would give the expression the largest interpretation. The Prime Minister's argument was that the Government elected in 1917 differed in no way from the government of 1904, let us say, which was elected on the question of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The cases are not at all similar. Had there been a sharp line of division, let us say within the Liberal party, on the question of the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if Sir Wilfred Laurier gone to gentlemen opposite and asked their concurrence for the special purpose of putting through legislation for the building of that railway, then the conditions might have been somewhat similar. The Prime Minister is not comparing things that are the same in nature. The only political situation we have had approach-

ing that which confronted the Canadian people at the time of the election in 1917 was the election in Canada prior to Confederation when Brown and certain Liberals of Ontario-quite a number of Liberals of Ontario-joined Macdonald and certain Tories of both Ontario and Quebec for the purpose of putting through Confederation, although Dorion and other Liberals in Quebec opposed him. That is apolitical situation which approximates somewhat the political situation of 1917. And what happened then ? It is very, very interesting, Mr. Speaker. As soon as Confederation was an assured fact Brown resigned, but Howland and MeDougall did not-they hung onto office. The name of Brown will be admired and revered in this country after generations have passed who have forgotten that there ever was a Howland or a MeDougall. We have with us today some Howlands and some McDougalls, although they bear different names. The Prime Minister said yesterday that the aim and objects of his Government are the same as those of the preceding administration. Well, if I wanted to be unkind I might admit it. I might say that the aim and objects of Union government were to retain power, and the aim and objects of this Government are to retain power. But let us be kinder. What were the declared and ostensible objects of Union government? The declared and ostensible objects of the government were to carry on, in a manner which they judged efficacious, the fighting of the war which was to maintain democracy and to crush privilege and autocracy. The declared aim of this Government is to hold on to office-to maintain autocracy and to maintain the protective principle in the tariff, which is to maintain privilege and autocracy as well.
In passing let me call attention to an error of fact into which the memory of the Prime Minister led him. In his remarks he stated that the Government had had large majorities on every vote last session.
I see a ray of hope there, Mr. Speaker, because if the Prime Minister thinks a majority of five large, what sort of majority is he counting upon in this vote? If my recollection is right, the Government majority last session was rarely more than twenty-five, and on one important occasion it dropped to five. But, after all, for a party which went into power with a majority of about seventy, majorities in the twenties or under were certainly small majorities.

Now, let us come to another phase of the subject. The Prime Minister has formed a Government which he describes as a National Liberal and Conservative Government-to put it in more popular phrase, a National Grit and Tory Government, which is about as wise and reasonable as "National Wet and Dry Government." I speak without the slightest personal experience, but as a matter of fact I understand it is quite possible for those who have been very dry to sometimes get very wet, and the day after the change they are very, very dry.
Hear, hear.

I hear sounds of "hear, hear" from the other side. I am glad my confirmation comes from that direction rather than from my own side of the House. <
The Prime Minister has arranged this Government with its long name of National Liberal and Conservative Government, and he has induced to join that Government the hon. member for Yarmouth and Clare (Mr. Spinney).
Now, what is a political party, Mr. Speaker? A political party is an association of men who have joined themselves together for the purpose of advancing the public interest of certain principles of policy which they hold in common. That is the sense of Burke's definition, and I think it is as good a definition as we have of what a political party is. What is the Cabinet? The Cabinet is the executive committee of such a party, chosen from men who have seats in this or the other House. It stands to reason that if men form a party they have to have similar views-not, of course, on all questions, that would be impossible, but on the main leading questions before the people a fortiori a Cabinet must have like similarity of views, and a Cabinet which has men in it of diverse views cannot give sound, constitutional, strong government to a country.
Now, if there is one thing that the Prime Minister has enunciated it has been the-protective principle. It is true there has not been that same bold front presented in all parts of the country. When he visited the beautiful Eastern Townships-part of which I have the honour to represent-he made a speech in the thriving industrial town of Sherbrooke and emphasised the maintenance of duties,-in other words, the maintenance of protective principles. When he got out to Winnipeg, after speaking about tariff revision and the report to be made thereon by the Minister of Fin-

ance (Sir Henry Drayton), he uttered a pious hope that the duties would he lowered. As far as my recollection serves me, there was no such pious hope expressed^ him in the 'city of Sherbrooke. But, after all, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has been a pretty consistent protectionist.
Now let us hear what his Minister without portfolio from the province of Nova Scotia (Mr. Spinney) said as late as last year, within a few months of his joining the Government of the Prime Minister. He stated:
I can only say that I regret that at this staee my hon. friend found it necessary to introduce his amendment, which comes at a very inopportune time. It has for its purpose, I assume the downfall of the Union Government, or their return to the country to get a fresh mandate from the people. I do not wish to criticise, but as I am an honest follower of the Union party, I must point out this fact, that since they have been in power I have followed them as a free trade or rather as a revenue tariff Liberal. I am that to-day, but I do not believe that any tariff for other than revenue purposes could be satisfactorily dealt with in this country at the present time.
Our progressive friends may declare for free trade. They have come out for free trade, but I do not see where they propose to raise the enormous revenue to carry out the heavy responsibilities resting upon this country to-day. It means raising between $500,000,000 and $600,000,000 at least. You cannot get that by direct taxation in this country. The people of Canada are not educated up to that. Neither are the financial resources of the country capable of responding to direct taxation. To my mind the idea is absolutely absurd. We have
to raise a certain percentage of our necessary revenue through customs taxation, entirely aside from any question of protection. The Minister of Finance has maintained his reputation for honesty, and I believe he fully intends to give this country what he has promised in the way of tariff revision. When that revision comes in, if it should have any earmarks of protection, if this Parliament is in existence at that time, they can bank on my opposing any such tariff.
The hon. member for Yarmouth and Clare, the minister without portfolio from the province of Nova Scotia, need not wait until the Budget comes down; he has his answer in the Address from the Throne, for that address consecrates the principle of protection which he pledged himself to oppose. There is just one of two things for my hon. friend to do; he should tell us that he has honestly changed his opinion and no longer stands for the principle of tariff for revenue, but for the principle of tariff for protection, and after telling us that he should go down by the sea and ask the men in his constituency whether they approve of his change of mind.
They would not.

If he does not do that, then it is for the Prime Minister to explain how, when he is nailing the colours of protection to the mast, he invites a free trader, such as the hon. member for Yarmouth and Clare, to form one of his Cabinet. I grant that the member for Yarmouth and Clare brings respectability, high business integrity and a good name to the Cabinet of which my right hon. and learned friend is Prime Minister. But I say that it is constitutionally improper, and that it is a piece of camouflage when he attempts to deceive the public by window dressing his Cabinet with the name of the minister without portfolio from the province of Nova Scotia for the purpose of justifying the sign over the door-"Liberal," as well as "National" and "Conservative."
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask the hon. member a question? Does he stand for the policy of the Liberal party between 1896 and 1911?

I stand, Mr. Speaker, for the policy of the Liberal party as laid down in the tariff plank of the Great National Liberal Convention held in August,
1919.	I would say with all kindness and courtesy that what the people are most interested in at the present time in regard to this matter is not where the member for Brome stands, but where the member for Yarmouth stands.
Just tell us.
In time; do not be impatient.

No doubt explanations will be in order and may be forthcoming.* It would be interesting to know whether the member for Yarmouth has converted the Prime Minister to his fiscal views or whether the Prime Minister has converted the member for Yarmouth to his.
The next item of Cabinet reconstruction about which I would like to talk for a few moments is the entry of the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr.. Wigmore). The Prime Minister was a little facetious the other day, or attempted to be a little facetious, at the expense of the leader of the Opposition in connection with the election- at St. John. I was there and I know something about it. My hon. and learned friend the Prime Minister endeavoured to draw comfort from the fact that he had been able to elect a man in the city of St. John. But there is not much comfort in that for the Prime Minister, because when the Min-

ister of Customs went before the good people of St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert, he said, Mr. Speaker, 

and oh, it burned itself into my consciousness, - "I stand not as a Liberal and not as a Conservative. I stand first in the interests of the port of St. John; next I stand in the interests of the people of St. John; then I stand in the interests of the province of New Brunswick, and after that of the Dominion of Canada." Now, this is not a free paraphrase of what the hon. gentleman said; I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is almost verbatim from the speech which he made shortly before I arrived in [DOT] that city

where the river flows both ways in the short space of twenty-four hours. However, lest what I have said be regarded as unfair, let me read from one of the papers supporting the Minister, the St. John Standard of Friday, September 10. It says:
What can Dr. Emery-
Dr. Emery was the Liberal candidate.
-do for the city that Mr. Wigmore cannot? Can he do anything at all? And if he were by any chance to find himself in Parliament repre-sentmg St. John, what amount of weight would his representations carry? If the electors of bt. John were to turn Mr. Wigmore down, then there would be an end, once and for all, of any hopes there may be of getting any more work done on the harbour or anything else that the city is interested m, from the present Government ; and as this Government is likely to be in power for several years yet,-
They are not too hopeful, those people down in St. John.
-St. John cannot afford to shut herself out in the cold indefinitely. St. John won't do it; her citizens will rally to the support of Mr. Wigmore with even more enthusiasm than they did three years ago-
As a matter of fact, they rallied to his support only to the extent of about half the enthusiasm they had demonstrated two or three years before.
-and he will see that they get what they want for their city, and that its shipping facilities shall be such as will enable it to handle the ever-increasing traffic that is coming and going through it year after year. Citizens, stand by Mr. Wigmore, and he will stand by the city.
It reminds me of the celebrated phrase in Pickwick Papers-" Pickwick and principle";-Wigmore and the harbour!
Other attempts Mr. Speaker, have been made at Cabinet reconstruction. We have had court laid to the province of Quebec.
Fishing expeditions.

The Prime Minister has developed a great love for the province

of Quebec, and the province of Quebec has said: " Oh, Arthur, this is so sudden." And he has answered: "I never told my love, but let concealment, like a worm in the bud, feed on my damask cheek." I am glad the Prime Minister has spoken kind words of the people of the province from which I come and of the race to which I do not belong, which I love. My only regret is that he waited until he was forty-five years of age and Prime Minister of this country before expressing, at least audibly, any such sentiments. But better late than never; So, fishing operations have begun under the control-under the, initiative almost-of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. (Mr. Ballantyne). Since the House rose in July last, there has been fishing, but it has been hook-and-line fishing, because you see, Mr. Speaker, the fish can be landed only in a boat with somewhat slender rod of a byelection. The tackle is somewhat light- in fact, the rod much too frail. We hear that after great efforts, one fish has been hooked but not landed in the boat. The tackle was too weak; the rod was not strong enough, and the poor fish is in this position-we often see it; a man is fishing; he has left his landing net at home; his tackle is not strong enough to lift the fish into the boat; he is drowning the fish; the mouth of the fish is above water, but the fish is not in the boat. It is desperately hard on the fish and of little profit to the fisherman. Let me say this to my right hon. friends: situated immediately opposite it is not a very elevated thing to be trying to bribe, by portfolios, your political opponents to enter your Cabinet. It is not what should be done. It has not been successful; I hope the attempt will be given up, But-and I say it with pride for the province from which I come-although these temptations have been held out to man after man on this side of the House, as yet there is no one from our side in the Cabinet which is presided over so ably by-
What Cabinet?

Was there a remark made? If so I did not catch it. I was referring to the Cabinet presided over by the present Prime Minister. I thought there was a remark made, Mr. Speaker; I am sorry if I have made a mistake. Perhaps it was a whisper-sotto voce.
The Prime Minister has endeavoured to taunt the Liberal party on its tariff attitude. He says that it is hard for him to find where the Liberal party stands on the tariff. If he has not already a copy, he

has only to apply to the National Liberal organization and he will be given, with that liberality of hand which distinguishes us, as many copies as he likes of the proceedings of the Liberal Convention of 1919. The Liberals, in convention assembled, laid down a tariff platform. That tariff platform is the policy of the Liberal party. By that platform we stand, and by that platform we shall win.
I do not purpose at this time imposing upon the House any long tariff discussion.
I see the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) looking at me. Ah, how well I remember that day in the summer of 1915 at Calgary when I made a speech in which I said that the tariff could not be wiped out over night and that we must proceed with caution, how he rose and berated me as a friend of the protectionist manufacturers of the East. I did not go quickly enough for him then. What has come over the spirit of his dream that he sits where he sits now? There are five main things that have to be considered in the tariff. There is the relief of the consumer. There is the directing of the capital and labour of the country into channels where they will bring forth the greatest economic return. There is the freeing of the people from the control of trusts and combines. Those are the three great objectives of a tariff revision. Then we have to consider the fact that for many years we have had this system of protection, and care and prudence must be used in reducing the tariff; and we must also consider the question of revenue. Those are the five great things we have in mind. Those are the five great things which have been looked after, taken care of, provided for, in the tariff policy of the Liberal party.
This is an important debate because upon it may rest the fate of the Ministry. It is a matter for the Prime Minister to consider whether for his own personal political fate he should refuse to go to the country. I suppose all thoughtful men in this Chamber will admit that Parliamentary institutions are on trial; that there are in the world to-day many people who say that Parliamentary institutions have not worked out as they should have done and that recourse should be had to direct action.
The other day-when I say the other day I am referring to what really happened several months ago-there was a rumour in Great Britain that war was to be engaged in with Russia, and the labour leaders in the Old Land said: We will
have no war with Russia; if you bring on war with Russia, we will down tools; we will stop the machine. With their opposition to war with Russia I am in most complete accord, but with the idea that one section of the community should, by economic force, be able to impose its will upon the rest of us, I have no sympathy whatever. But there are only two ways in which men can be governed- 4 p.m. either by force or by their consent-and in order to have men governed by their consent, there must be an organization for giving that consent, that opinion, proper expression, there must be a maintenance of' some sort of Parliament; and any one who attempts to make Parliament unresponsive to the will of the people does so at the risk of encouraging direct action. I have no dislike in my heart for the Prime Minister; I admire his good qualities; but with his political practices and policies I am at eternal war. I believe he sits there a usurper, and I would remind him that no usurper has ever for long successfully controlled the destinies of a British country. There was one great usurper-his name was Cromwell-and he did a great deal for his country. He made the name of England known and respected on land and sea; but after he disappeared, his power immediately became as naught, and we had the Restoration with all its attendant ills. I would ask the Prime Minister to read the history of leaders in all democratic countries who held on to office once their right to office had terminated. Did not every one of them suffer and suffer badly for having done so? I believe history will show that I am right.
Just in conclusion, I have a word to submit in connection with the Liberal Unionists who yet sit on the side of the Government. With us they are or have been the inheritors of a great tradition and a great name. Every man of them got vote after vote, tens of votes, hundreds of votes, thousands of votes, on the distinct understanding that his mandate was for the war and for the war alone. If they sit there, if they support this Government, then they break their pledged word to the electors of the country who supported them on that understanding. They can do that, but it will be wrong. The other day I heard a story of that great explorer, missionary, scientist, David - Livingstone. He fell sick in the centre of Africa; he was carried to the coast by his African bearers, and when he reached the coast there was an

English ship that would have taken him home to glory, honour, safety and health. But he had given his word to those Africans that he would take them back home again to their native village, and he left health, life and the opportunity for glory; he kept his word to those Africans, and they bore him back into mid-Africa to die because he was a man of his word, because his plighted word to him was above everything else. The fate of this Government is in the hands of those men who formerly called themselves Liberals, who sit behind the Government. It will be for them to say whether there should be an immediate appeal to the* people or whether this Government should maintain itself in power after having secured power under an understanding that its mandate would cease with the war.	'

Mr. Speaker, every member who rises in his seat in this House to address his fellow-members generally asks for the indulgence of those who are about to listen to his remarks. This is specially true to-day on account of the special circumstances I am in, and I shall not even wait for the indulgence of my fellow-members, I ask for it at the very outset of my remarks. '
I should not like to be discourteous towards the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McMaster). He has spoken m a very light manner indeed of the procedure adopted by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government to secure representation in the Cabinet. I should not like to follow him in- the same vein, but I shall address a few remarks to that hon. gentleman. He concluded his address with an appeal to the Liberal members who are supporting the Government, so that dissolution of Parliament could be secured. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Brome claims to be a Liberal, claims to love justice, claims to fight for fair play, and represents one of the constituencies of the province of Quebec. And yet he has the audacity to rise in this House and in the name of his constituents ask the Government to dissolve Parliament when, according to the constitution the province of Quebec is the pivot of Confederation, and when its last unit of representation was 30,080, while its unit of representation based on the next census will in view of the increase as shown by the records of our province be 40,000 dollars.
Oh, oh.

Yes, some of my
fellow members laugh when I speak of dollars. I would like those who laugh and those who smile to be able to stand where I stand to-day and fight the battle that I am fighting. Laughter and smiles won't stop me. The men who have tried to tame me know they cannot tame or break me. I was saying that our unit of representation based on the next census will be 40,000. Take simply the Island of Montreal, represented in this Parliament by twelve members, and having a population of more than 800,000. The city of Montreal will be entitled to twenty seats. And yet a member from this province asks the Liberals supporting the Government to consent to the House being dissolved.
My hon. friend has been talking of fish and bribery. I do not know what he means, and I will wait for his future explanation. But when he says that he is going to stand on the platform of the Liberal party as enacted in the National Liberal Convention held in Ottawa in the month of August 1919, I would remind the House that the only plank which was able to bear the weight of the hon. member for Brome was the plank of free trade.
But since that convention was held, the plank has been so much chopped up that now it does not carry the hon. member but he carries it, cut in pieces, in his vest pocket. May I remind the hon. gentleman who is still labouring under the misapprehensions with which he prefaced his remarks on the question of free trade and protection, that it is only last year the hon. gentleman discovered that the Liberal party in its fifteen years of power had always adhered to protection. It was a scene to be recorded in Hansard, Mr. Speaker. Many Liberal members were sitting around the table, and the hon. member for Brome was trying to commit his party to free trade. The meeting was presided over by that great old politician warrior who for fifteen years sat on the treasury benches as Minister of Finance in the Laurier Administration. My hon. friend the member for Brome was trying to induce the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) to commit himself to free trade and said " Well, does not the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's understand that the Liberal party is a party of free traders?" " Yes, yes," said the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's with his genial smile and in his highly cultured manner, " yes, yes, free trade is a nice theory." " But," said the member for Brome " we must have it." " Yes, yes,"

answered the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's," " In theory; hut in practice, no." The hon. member for Brome was dumbfounded. He had still ringing in his ears all the speeches of the Liberal chieftain stating that the Liberals were for free trade. But he had not looked at the statute book. He did not realize until last year that when in power his party and my party adhered to the protectionist idea, as can he proven. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, I should not take up more time in discussing the hon. member for Brome. Perhaps in the course of my remarks I may have the pleasure of referring to him once more.
I come now to the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin). He issues a warning to the Government. He says: Do not talk tariff on the Address. Who is talking tariff on the Address? The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) stated that he was ready to discuss the tariff question. As a matter of fact, he said: Whenever our party comes back to power we will give this country a tariff identical with that of the fifteen years of Liberal Administration. Now what was the platform of that party if it was not protection? Mr. Speaker, when the Liberal party came into power in 1896 the platform of the National Liberal Convention of 1893 was still fresh in the minds of everybody. The Liberal leader at that time, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, called in to his assistance all the Liberal premiers of the different provinces of Canada, and we had in this country what will go down in our political history as the great Cabinet of Confederation. What happened, Sir? In spite of all the pledges for "free trade as they had it in England," and all the promises that the tariff should be a tariff for revenue only, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's had a tariff commission going around the country just as the present Government has had a commission going around the country.
And I do not understand why the member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) should ask the question, "Why a tariff question?" When the party which he supports had two commissions, one in 1897 and another in 1907. The fact is that this Government is following the same policy as the Liberals followed when they were in power. I admit that there were many articles on the free list; I do not remember the exact number, but speaking from memory I believe that there were at least 141 articles on the free list; and the duties were lower-on at least 118 articles coming
from foreign countries into Canada. But there was a preferential duty accorded British industry. The first preferential duty was 25 per cent, and it was understood that it would be increased to 33 1-3 per cent. If my figures are correct the tariff of 1897 when brought down was an average tariff of 21 per cent. Now, in the devastation that follows war the countries that have suffered must import farm products from those countries that have continued to produce. The demand arising from South Africa after the war in that country arose about the same time as the preference was given by us to British industry, and these two combined caused a condition of expansion and development in Canada.
Here I desire to draw attention to a fact that tells many sad tales. In 1893 the Hon. Joseph Israel Tarte fought his Conservative friends. He threw down the gauntlet to his former associates to run in the County of L'lslet on the question of the Connolly Dry Dock Scandal. He was returned, to battle down the fortress of the Conservative party in this House, and finally brought Parliament to dissolution in 1896. Every man of my age who had the opportunity to fight in those days must remember the Hon. Mr. Tarte who, during the Campaign of 1896 had not enough money to pay his cab fare from one meeting to another. They must remember the hard work he did and I think they will recall the fact that he was rewarded in a sense, by being appointed Minister of Public Works. But the Liberals of that day, like the so-called Liberals of to-day, wanted to secure the scalp of Mr. Tarte and represented him as a Tory in a Liberal Government. In 1904-and here is the injustice of the thing ___Mr. Tarte started a campaign preaching the increase of tariff duties, because in the meantime the British Preference had gone up to 33 1-3 per cent, and our industries were unable to compete. As I stand here, Sir, I have no hesitation in saying that the woollen industry of this country has been killed by the British Preference; but for the sake of the rest of the community we swallowed the Preference and the woollen industry went bankrupt. Seeing the danger with which this country was confronted, Mr. Tarte started a campaign to have the tariff raised; he preached the increase of protection. He was thrown out of the Cabinet, and in 1907, three years after his expulsion, this very party increased the tariff from 21 per cent to 29

per cent, the very thing which Mr. Tarte had been advocating. Listen to their speeches! They have saved the country! Yes, Sir, they saved the country-when they could not do otherwise. Imagine my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) speaking as he does, when he knows that for fifteen years the Liberal party had been committed to protection. Imagine his being the financial critic of the Opposition during a whole Parliament. God save that party! The Conservatives of this country have been committed to the principle of protection since 1878; and the proof that the Liberal party had a protective tariff is the fact that during the elections of 1911 the Tories said "let well enough alone." They were satisfied with the tariff at that time. What has happened since? Since 1911 the British Preference has been abolished. I do not believe that the present Government should be lauded for this. The tariff has been reduced to please the agrarian movement, and I do not believe either that the Government should be lauded on this account. Sir, let me make a declaration here and now: I have more respect for the representatives of the farmer and the labour elements because they are true to the doctrines they preach. There is a difference between this group on the cross benches and that other group, the Liberal group. The Liberals vary their declaration as they move from one parish to another, from one county to another, and from one province to another. The hon. gentleman who represents the county of Maisonneuve and at the same time the county of Gaspe has declared in the province of Quebec time and time again that he was a protectionist, that he always had been a protectionist, and that his party was one that adhered to the principle of protection. Yet he was present at the convention, where he spoke, and two rows behind him the hon. member for Brome could stand up and say: "I am a free trader; I am against protection"-this notwithstanding that his provincial leader called himself a protectionist to the core.
Well, Sir, if-as I believe and as I think will be admitted-the Liberal party when in power adhered to protection; and if the Liberal party, as has been stated by the member for North Cape Breton when brought back to power, is willing to give the country a tariff similar to that of the Liberal administration from 1896 to 1911, why should the Opposition now refuse to accept the paragraph in the speech from the Throne with respect to protection? Ah,

they are trying to evade the point, they are trying to cloud the issue that is involved, they do not care about the other provinces. The Liberal party in this House numbers eighty-two members, and sixty-one of them come from the province of Quebec. In that province they control or are interested in certain newspapers, and they believe that through the influence of those journals they will be able to so mould public opinion as to ensure that the solid block of Liberal members from Quebec shall never be disintegrated. On this issue I am prepared to meet them, if not through the press on the public platform.

We will be there.
Other hon. MEMBERS: We will meet you.

To hear these hon. gentlemen one would imagine that I held the fate of the Government in my hands and that they were asking for dissolution from me. The answer I give them is that I promise to transfer their message to the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government.	*
A good messenger

A messenger that the Liberal party was glad to have in its ranks for many years; a messenger who in their interest ran from one to another of the forty-five ridings in the district of Montreal and who has preached the gospel of Liberalism not only in Quebec but in New Brunswick, in Ontario and in the West; a messenger that my hon. friends can use no more; a messenger that they are willing still to be master of but who recognizes no master since his leader is dead.
Coming to the question of dissolution the leader of the Opposition wishes to know what mandate the Government has for remaining in office. Sir, I have always thought that according to sound constitutional doctrine a government was elected for the period prescribed by the law- that it was at liberty to shorten that period, but had no power to enlarge it. That is the letter of the law. What is the spirit of the law? It is that as long as a government has a majority in this Chamber it can remain in office, and many are the occasions when it should undoubtedly do so. Supposing the appeal made by the hon. member for Brome should be favourably received by Liberals who are now supporting the Government? Supposing for one moment that were to occur

and that those thirty-eight Liberal members were to cross to the Opposition side? Would the leader of the Opposition when called into office be obliged to go to the country?
Sure.

No, he would have
supporting him a majority of the members elected for this Parliament. Possibly he might take that course, but it is my firm belief that if such a thing happened he would not go to the country. He would not go to the country because if he did so in advance of the redistribution of seats following the taking of the census he would not remain in office for one single day. The West, as well as the province of Quebec, would clamour to have its rights; and no Prime Minister would be strong enough to withstand the clamour that would be raised by the province of Quebec supported by the other provinces.
But there is another consideration to be borne in mind. At the last session of Parliament the Opposition proposed an amendment to the Speech from the Throne declaring that the Government had no mandate and that it should dissolve Parliament and go to the people.

Did you support that
amendment?
I did.

Why have you
changed your attitude then?

Do not be to precipitate. I will give my explanation and it will show the difference between the hon. members of the Opposition and myself. I will prove that I am consistent and that they are not. But inconsistency does not worry my hon. friends; they never were consistent. When the amendment declaring that the Government had no mandate had been debated and the division had disclosed beyond no doubt that it had sufficient majority to continue transacting the affairs of the country, what happened? Towards the close of the session a resolution increasing the indemnity of members was brought down and adopted. Did my hon. friends of the Opposition accept that increase? Yes, Sir, they did. Why did they accept it if the Government had no mandate? If their contention were true, they, as well as the Government and its supporters, improperly accepted money from the public treasury. But they accepted the increase of indemnity, and having done so they now say to the Government which
granted it, "You have no mandate, get out." Last Session I voted in favour of the motion declaring the Government had no mandate, but I accepted the increase of indemnity because the majority decided otherwise and to that position I adhere.
I did not benefit by the increase of indemnity.

I was going to make an exception with respect to my hon. friend; I should be very sorry not to do so. The only gentleman who stood up in this House and fought the increase of indemnity was the hon. member for Laprairie and Napierville (Mr. Lanctot). Of course, like the others, he pocketed the ' money, but he declared-and this is the declaration that I want- to underline-that he would never profit by this increase, but would divide it equally between his two counties. I suppose that is what he intends to do. The auditors will audit the books, and they will report in due time.
Mr. Speaker, will you permit me to offer an explanation?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is not in order in making an explanation at this stage. If he desires to submit a question to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rou-ville (Mr. Gauthier) he may do so with the latter's consent.

The gentleman who wanted to correct stands corrected. The hon. member (Mr. McMaster) seemed to be very fond of precedents to show that this Government might remain in office. Of course, hon. members of the Opposition have stated that there is no precedent whatever for such retention of power. May I be permitted, Sir, to tell hon. members who come from my province that the only two precedents that can be quoted occurred in our own native province. In November, 1904, we had a provincial election there. The Premier at that time was the late Hon. S. N. Parent, and he had as one of his cabinet ministers Mr. Lomer Gouin. The election was fought in November, the cabinet of Mr. Parent was maintained, and the House was called upon to meet in January; but for fifteen days there were no sittings, because the members were fighting in groups, and finally Mr. Gouin got the best of it and Mr. Parent was murdered, politically. Is that a precedent? The Liberals still claim that Sir Lomer Gouin is the greatest premier we have ever had in our province, but that

is the way he came into power. He had no mandate from the people; he had a mandate from the members of the House, and that was sufficient for him, and was also sufficient for the federal members, the so-called Liberals from Quebec.
But there is another precedent, Sir;' it happened in 1920. In June, 1919, we had a general election for the provincial House. Sir Lomer Gouin was the premier, and was returned with seventy-six of his partisans, but later on he was appointed to the Legislative Council and Mr. Tasche-reau took his place. Mr. Taschereau did not go to the country. Is not that a precedent? "Oh, well," the Liberal press of Quebec will Bay, "he is following the same policy." He is not, and they know it. Sir Lomer Gouin had placed on the statute books a prohibition law. Mr. Taschereau is about to enact another law by which the local government at Quebec will he the absolute and sole dealer in alcohol. Is that the same policy as Sir Lomer Gouin's? No. Did Mr. Taschereau go to the country? No.
Having disposed of the arguments that have been advanced so far by those who fight this Government on the question of dissolution, to please my former friends I should like to go a lttle deeper into politics. I asked the indulgence of the House. As there was no expression of dissent, I suppose I secure that indulgence. The Liberals of to-day, as I stated a moment ago, do not follow the path of true Liberalism. What constitutes the first principle of Liberalism? It is universal suffrage. Who gave it to this country, the Liberals or the Conservatives? I was amazed to listen to my hon. friend from Brome, a worthy scion of the sturdy Scotch race. I suppose he came originally from the Highlands, but he has always lived in the lowlands of politics. He proclaims himself a Liberal of the old school, and yet in his speech, Sir, he was complaining because during the war the Government of the day saw fit to give the right to vote to the wives and daughters of the soldiers at the front. From a Liberal standpoint it was a good move to give universal suffrage; but it came from the Government of the day, consequently my hon. friend from Brome sets aside his Liberalism and hurls his attacks against the Government.
Liberals of to-day, we will-with your permission, Mr. Speaker-look over the road. The Liberal party in days gone by fought for many years to abolish the double mandate, and it was finally abolished in 1873. 
Before that year the same man could be a senator, a legislative councillor, and an appointee of the Crown. This double mandate had emanated from the Family Compact, which at one time controlled this country for the advantage of the few. What do you see, Sir, even in this Chamber? You see the hon. member for St. Denis, Montreal (Mr. Verville), the untamed defender of the working man. Do you remember, Sir, his fiery speeches when he was cutting into small bits a piece of sausage to distribute to the children? He was preaching rebellion, and I remember having heard him say on the floor of the House, when we were discussing the $35,000,000 grant to the English navy, that if ever there was a war the working men would stop it by going on strike. Well, he was a very bad prophet, as he is a very bad Liberal. Actually he draws his sessional indemnity of $4,000 as a member of this House, and he draws $10,000 as a commissioner of the city of - Montreal. When he is in Montreal he does not fulfil his duties in Ottawa; when he is m Ottawa he does not fulfil his duties in Montreal. But he draws the two salaries. He is for the double mandate as long as he can hold on to it.
He is not alone, Sir; he has a colleague who stands in the same position. I might say, en passant, that the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) is at the same time a member of the House and a substitute for the Attorney General at Montreal at a salary of $4,000. But when the late Government appointed Mr. Cha-pais to the Senate, while at the same time he held the office of Legislative Councillor, you could hear the Liberals claiming that it was an outrage. An outrage when the double mandate is for the benefit of the Tories, but a mighty good thing when it is for the benefit of one of the Liberals.
But in this House, Sir, we have better than that. We have an hon. member, who, since the beginning of this Parliament has represented two different ridings separated by a distance of three hundred and fifty miles. One is the constituency of Maison-neuve, which is an urban riding; the other is the constituency of Gaspe, mostly settled by fishermen. When the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) is asked by the fishermen of Gaspe to support a policy of free trade because they want to obtain American goods free of duty as well as enjoy the benefits of the Boston market for their fish, the hon. member has to advocate free trade. But when the electors of Maison-

neuve want protection because with free trade their earning power might be diminished, the hon. gentleman votes for protection. Whether it is free trade or protection, the hon. member is sure always to have one seat at the right time. The member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe has been in public life for quite a while. He has a few friends-a few people are scared by him; and a large number of people do not care much about him. By right of seniority he is the first lieutenant of the provincial Liberal wing. The member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is at the head of the other faction. If -I were to compare the leaders of the two factions, I would say that the members in the Quebec district are proud of their leader in the person of the member for Quebec East; but who among those of the Montreal district will say that he is proud of his leader? I do not think, Sir, that you could find one who would say so. Why? The hon. member was described on one occasion in a newspaper article published in French, entitled " Tout pour le mieux ". If I had. to translate this in English I would say:	" All to the good," but
in order to get at its real meaning in this case I would have to translate it: "Everything for Lemieux." That is why the hon. member has no friends, Mr. Speaker. And pretending to represent the Liberal party, though he was not the leader of the party to which I belonged, has seen fit to read me out of the ranks of the Liberal Party. I have been in the Liberal Party since 1896. I' have fought the battles of my party since 1897. I never complained when I was given the worst positions to defend; I never complained when there were any bouquets or flowers to receive that were received by others. No, Sir, I never complained. I was a soldier in the Liberal army and I did my duty to the best of my ability and according to the dictates of my conscience. The hon. gentleman has no right to say that I am a traitor; that I am a renegade; that I am a Judas. He has no right, either, to ask his fellow-members who are the owners or editors of certain newspapers in my Province to hurl insults at me, after all I have dong for every one of them.
I am going to try to show who is really the traitor and renegade. I stand here for the protective tariff as enacted by the Liberal administration. For what does the Liberal Opposition stand? Fifteen per cent tariff; fifty per cent Imperial preference-giving a preference of seven and a half per cent against English industries, and in favour of our own industries. Who are the traitors? Who are the renegades? Is the man a traitor who still fights for the tariff instituted by the late Sir Wilfred Laurier and the Liberal Party, which has brought wealth and happiness to the people? Or are those the traitors who went to destroy that platform; who want free trade; who want a tariff for revenue, or any kind of policy which will enable them to take the spoils of office?
I was elected as a Laurierite in 1917. On what policy, Sir? On the Laurier naval policy. For that policy I stand and will stand to the end of my political life. Am I a traitor? Am I a renegade? Am I a Judas? Whom have I betrayed? The Liberal Opposition themselves have left the platform and the policy of Laurier. I was elected by electors who knew where I stood and who know where I stand to-day. To whom am I a traitor? In what respect am I a renegade? Against whom am I a Judas? Where is the man, where is the party, where is the platform, that I have betrayed? It cannot be shown. But in order to keep the Quebec block solid, the two factions of the Liberals of the province of Quebec do not want any conferences between Quebec and the Government. They admit, though, that Quebec, being in the minority, must have an ally. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) would be willing to join hands with the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). The hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe is willing, if I can rely upon his word, to make an alliance with the Hon. Mr. Drury. Everyone admits that the isolation of Quebec must be terminated; but because I do not see eye to eye with my hon. friends, because I do not want to be a party to an alliance with the farmers, to an alliance with the labourers, because I am afraid of the communism of the agrarian movement-
Oh no, we are all right.

I have a right to my opinion even when it is contradicted by the hon. member for Red Deer. I do not want him to be ruled by my opinion, and he could not ask me to be ruled by his. It is my belief, Sir, that the agrarian movement is tending to a class movement, and I am afraid of that, and my people are afraid of it. Have we not a right to

choose our ally? Are we going to choose our ally to please Mr. So-and-So or the hon. member for such-an-such riding? We are going to seek an alliance, this alliance to be made for the benefit of all parties concerned and specially for harmony amongst all classes, all groups, all provinces, all races, all creeds.
When the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) took exception to my words, I was stating that I could not advocate an alliance with the labour element. I will say why. The labour element in this country is affiliated with the American Federation of Labour, the headquarters of which are at Washington, pretty near the Capitol. I do not want our policy, our fiscal policy, our national policy, to be dominated by somebody who does not live in our land. That is quite right, and I have an absolute right to hold that opinion. I have said this, and I am willing to repeat it because I speak the truth as I understand it. I have more respect for the farmers who stand by their guns, who advocate free trade, who want to have a group of agrarian members in this House. We know where they are; we know where they will land. I can discuss matters with them, because I know what they want; I am not afraid of them; they are under their own flag, they show their colours. We know of what stamp they are made; we know what their policy is. But after all, if their principles do not agree with my belief, surely I am at liberty to say that I do not want an alliance- with that group.
Mr, CLARK (Red Deer) : Sure.

Thank you. Before leaving this interesting subject of the Liberalism of the Liberals of to-day, I should like to make a few more references to my bosom friend, the hon. member who represents in this House the two constituencies of Gaspe and Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). In this life majority counts; we must have every unit when we are fighting. Here is a gentlemen who is supposed to
5 p.m. be a Liberal, who holds in this House a double mandate with only one seat.	The Liberal party has
found its last refuge in the province * of Quebec, because outside of Quebec, I do not believe there are more than twenty-one Liberal members. The Liberal party, when the votes are recorded, is interested in having all the votes it can poll; but . through sheer eogtism the hon. gentleman has seen fit to keep the two seats, and
 *
whenever a vote is recorded, the Opposition loses one vote. But my hon. friend wants to go down to posterity as having been on the same footing as his late chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who for one Parliament held two seats also. But one of those seats was protested before the courts; actually there is no protest. How is it that a gentleman can stand in that position for the satisfaction of his own feeling against the triumph or the progressive fight of the party with which he is affiliated? It is a mystery which cannot be very easily explained. If I had any malicious feeling towards the hon. gentleman, I would say that I could give two explanations of his career, one a literary one and the other an applied science one. In reading over the fables of LaFontaine one finds the Fable of the Bat. The Bat, when flying with birds, can say: "Look at my wings, I am a bird," but when down on mother earth, she can also say: "I am a mouse; long live the rodents." When the hon. gentleman fights for free trade, he appeals to the masses of democracy td look at his wings. But when he fights for the big interests of his own constituency, when he goes with the bankers, the financiers, the industrial men; when he goes into the trust companies, into the insurance companies, dealing with all the wealthy in the land-"long live the rodents." If, passing from this literary reminiscence you go to applied science, you will remember that for many years there was a great discussion about airships. Some scientists claimed that in order to float in the atmosphere you should have something lighter than air. Then scientists came to the conclusion that it was necessary to have something heavier than air. At the time of the first theory balloops were made of silk and were filled with gas. Then the aeroplane was invented, and through the rapidity of the movements ofl its motor it was able to plane into the atmosphere. The hon. gentleman started his career as a balloon. He was robed with silk and filled with gas. Then he changed into an aeroplane. He had to give action to his airship through the most powerful motor there has ever been in this land, one that can never be duplicated. This motor was named Sir Wilfrid Laurier. When the motor stopped, the aeroplane . came down to Mother Earth, and it is still splashing around in all the muddy spots, whence it can fly no more. He can say to those who still surround him: "Once I was

a bird, look at my broken wings," but for the common people he will ever remain the most perfect political bat this country has ever known or heard of.
Mr. Speaker, it is an unsound Liberalism to preach the gospel of hatred against the majority of a country. It is unsound Liberalism to isolate a minority in a country.
Hear, hear.

Oh, never mind. This is a very serious game, and I have had to discard the hon. gentleman. There is no joker in the deck. I repeat, it is unsound Liberalism to isolate a minority, and. I stand by what I have just said. It may be all right to have a solid block if you can appeal to the majority and win them to your cause, but if you cannot win them on account of your platform or on account of your theory, and if you are condemned to remain an isolated minority, I say it is bad Liberalism, and that has been proved to the hilt by the constitutional history of this country. The doctrine is so false that even the so-called Liberals are looking for allies. They are trying to induce the farmers to come in with them. They feel their utter incapacity unless they make an alliance. With whom should this alliance be made? By whom should it be made? These are the two points I should like to discuss now.
I have advocated the doctrine that isolation for Quebec should come to an end. Have I sacrificed any one of my political principles? Not one. Have I betrayed anybody? No one. If there are those in my province who are in any better position to discuss the situation with the powers that sit on the Treasury Benches, why do they not discuss it? If they believe that an alliance should be made, and if the Government of to-day is willing to make an alliance on a fair basis, with equal rights and mutual respect for everybody, who should complain? The policy of an alliance has been the policy of Quebec since the days of 1840 under the Union Act. It has been the sound policy, and it cannot be otherwise, for the good of this country, and the interests of all parties are looked after.
Sir, we have had two policies of alliances in this country. I am speaking now of my own province. The province of Quebec has had two alliances, one was when Cartier united Quebec with Ontario. The other was after 1896 when my late leader made an alliance between Quebec and the West. If you look at the records of the general elections of 1900, 1904, 1908, 1911, and
1917, you will see that, although through the alliance of the late Clarke Wallace with the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we were able to get forty-eight out of the ninety-six seats in Ontario, at every ensuing general election this majority has dwindled. It was thirty-eight in 1904, it was less than twenty in 1908, it came down to seventeen in 1911, and it finally rested at thirteen. What is the meaning of this? It is that the province of Ontario, seeing that the alliance with Quebec had been broken for the benefit of the western provinces, sought new alliances to direct the policies of this country. The alliance between Cartier and Macdonald was consummated in 1849 or 1850, about the time when the Governor General was insulted in the streets of Montreal, when the Parliament building was set on fire, when the annexation manifesto was circulated and signed by many people in this country who wanted secession from the mother country and annexation with the United States.
Cartier made an alliance with Macdonald. What has been the result so far as the country and my province are concerned? We had the opening of the La-chine canal, the construction of the Grand Trunk railway, the abolition of " tenure seigneuriale" in 1854, the organization of our municipal law in 1858. We had the codification of our French laws in 1864, and then there was Confederation, which gave to the province of Quebec the absolute control of all matters relating to education and of parochial and municipal law, making Quebec mistress in her own territory, under the guidance of the Federal Parliament.
This is what we had under the first alliance. What have we from the other one, and what can we expect? That is the point. The population of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, is atached to the soil. This is our own country; we have no other. If we left it we should be exiles. We must therefore remain here; we are rooted to the soil. It was discovered by our forefathers; it was trodden by our pioneers, and it has been reddened with the blood of our martyrs. We want to remain here; therefore, we have no desire to go ony-where else. Now, we are in the minority. With whom should we make an alliance? I have claimed all along that the natural ally of Quebec is Ontario. Since 1912, after the defeat of reciprocity in 1911, in the ranks of my own party I have advocated that theory and preached it as a gospel. I was not listened to. The Liberal party



wants to retain an alliance with the West. Sir, I have no objection to the people of the West:	none at all. I respect them.
They came here to draw from the soil the wealth which Providence has stored there for those who are sturdy enough to work and obtain it. I have no objection to their helping us to develop the country. But, Mr. Speaker, figures are figures, and I have before me figures that show that west of the Great Lakes 63 per cent of the population are not British born. This is not my fault, but it is a fact. Am I going to preach an alliance with those who have not the same ideals as we have and who do not love our institutions? No, Sir, I cannot do that; for one, I will not consent to it. Everyone, of course, is at liberty to choose his own ally. I am choosing mine, and I shall try to make my people see as I do in this matter. If I fail I shall not bewail my failure; but I hope to win because I want to see peace and harmony restored in this country. This doctrine, in my mind, is a sound one. It is not based on prejudice; it is not based on hatred; it is not based on any sad passion of the human heart. The doctrine was so sound that my former friends, the so-called Liberals, could not attack it, and they therefore decided to murder the preacher.
Now, they have begun to take cognizance of two accusations that have been levelled at me, one since 1906, and the other since 1915. At the outset of my remarks I asked for the indulgence of the House, as it was my intention to deal once for all with those accusations; and if my former friends, so-called Liberals, have seen fit to make use of those accusations, being a public man, I have considered that the proper place in which to dispose of them is the House of Commons, the highest tribunal in the land. I shall deal with the first accusation.
It is that in 1906, when I ran as a Liberal candidate for the county of L'Assomp-tion, I promised my support to the Conservative party in consideration of the sum of $1,500 which was to be paid to me. This accusation has been hurled against me now for fifteen years. So long as the Conservatives of my province thought fit to make use of that charge I deemed it a good strategic move to let them keep on for the time being, for they were not injuring the governments which I was supporting. As a matter of fact, Sir, this charge has never hurt me, because every time it has been made I have been in a position to give the official denial to it. Here are the facts. In 1906 there was a vacancy in the Provin-

cial House, ocasioned by the appointment of Mr. Joseph P. Duhamel to the office of Chief Registrar of the province. The Liberal convention held at L'Assomption was presided over by the late Hon. Jean Provost, who was at the time Minister of Colonization and of Marine and Fisheries in the local Cabinet. My name was put forward as a candidate to the convention. I refused to have my name put up for nomination because I was certain-I had the proof -that some delegates had been approached with the view of inducing them to vote against me; and not wishing to be slaughtered by process of a convention organized and influenced in that way, I withdrew my name before nomination.
One Joseph Papin was chosen as the candidate. He was the President of the Agricultural Society of the County, but his choice did not meet with the approval of the farming community. Immediately after he was chosen, some farmers came to me and tendered me the nomination should I desire to run as an independent Liberal. One of those farmers offered me his personal cheque for $1,200 to defray my expenses. On the morning of nomination day the man chosen as the government candidate was so strong that he ran away and I was returned by acclamation. Now, Sir, the Conservatives since that time have spread broadcast against me, the slander that they had been prepared to bribe me.
I will explain how this legend has been created. The Provincial Government of the day was preparing a taxation law against fraternal societies. La Soeiete des Artisans Canadiens Frangais, which is doing business in eight provinces of Canada and in eight states of the American Union would have been called upon, had the proposed legislation been enacted, to pay in taxation an amount equal to six or seven thousand dollars, whereas they were at the time paying but a nominal tax. In the law of every province of Canada, or state of the United States, there is a proviso that if a foreign company doing business in that province or in that state is paying in its own country a higher taxation than it is paying in the foreign country, the government of the latter country will have the privilege of increasing its taxation to an amount equal to that imposed in the native land of the association. The proposed legislation would have meant for this society a taxation of from five to six thousand dollars a year, when we were paying but $5 and $10 a year in every provinee and state.

The lawyer of the Society was one Alfred Labelle, who is now deceased. During the time of the L'Assomption election we discussed more than once the question of the taxation of the fraternal societies. I was interested in La Societe des Artisans, and Mr. Labelle and I decided that if it were necessary we would organize a joint movement between all the fraternal societies doing business and having their headquarters in the province of Quebec so that we would be able to ask the government to refrain from putting the proposed law into effect. Well, Sir, J was returned by acclamation. Afterward I went and had dinner at the Club Lafontaine, which was a social as well as a business club. My leader, Sir Lomer Gouin, had dinner there more than once. Lately in the city of Montreal a banquet was given to a certain Conservative senator who was attended by Liberal senators, and even ministers, men who were personal friends of the host. Would it be possible to suppose for one moment that because you have a luncheon or a dinner with a man of opposite politics you are going to betray your party? That is nonsense.
