I did not need the money. I was returned by acclamation. If I had been opposed I had actually a certain amount of money which was more than sufficient to pay my legal expenditure. I did not need the money, I did not get the money, I never promised anything. After the election I was asked by the then Premier to propose the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne. Since that day up till last fall I always fought for my party, and have defended members of the Liberal party when Conservatives were attacking them. Now so-called Liberals, my former friends, are indulging in slanderous attacks. The only thing I can say that I have nothing but contempt for them and for their actions.
Now, Mr, Speaker, let me proceed to the second acccusation. It is the one which has reference to the same Society of Artisans. The Society was founded in 1817, in the dark hour of that dark period when the civic authorities in the city of Montreal were compelled to open public kitchens at the corners of all thoroughfares to feed the starving population. [DOT] A carpenter by the name of Archambault founded the Society to look after the interests of sick members and, upon their demise, the interests of their widows and orphans. As in the case of all societies of the kind funded during that century, it was based on charity and sympathy.
Orginally the Society was local in its character, but, starting in 1890, it expanded throughout all the provinces, and in 1900 it began operations in the United States. I regret to say that although in 1915 the membership was forty-three thousand and that membership international in character, its administration was provincial in the sense that all the directors to be elected must be chosen in the district of Montreal. I entered the Society in 1900. I acted as a delegate at the convention of that year and have acted in a similar capacity at every convention since. I have been in charge of the legislative committee which has entirely transformed the Society and its finances and which has put the Association-to quote the words of its actuary Mr. George Dyre Aldridge [DOT]-in a position unique on the whole continent. When I left the office of president, to which I was elected in 1914, for every $100 of liability I left in the coffers of the association $125.50. The Society stands in a class by itself. After having transformed this society, I was the first professional man to be elected as first vice-president, which office consists mostly in looking after the financial affairs of the association. At the convention of 1914 I was the first professional man to be elected to the high office of president, and I am sure that office was given to me unanimously on account of the services that I had rendered to the society.
Now, Sir, on the first Saturday of September, 1915, just as I was leaving the hospital where I had been undergoing an operation, the newspaper Le Pays came out with an article stating that L. J. Gauthier had been speculating with the funds of the society, that he had taken the money in its treasury to buy bonds, which he afterwards re-sold to the society of which he was the president. This was the accusation, and it was afterwards published in the Montreal newspaper, La Patrie, by the Quebec newspaper, L'Evene-ment, and also by Le Courrier de St. Hya-cinthe, which at the time was a Conservative organ.
A convention was called, and the membership of 43,000 sent in their delegates. The books were opened and the transactions carefully examined, and out of sixty-five votes, eleven were cast against me and fifty-four were given in my favour, the latter stating that the accusation was malicious, slanderous and unfounded. But I was not surprised. The society being international in its membership and provin-

Is it possible, Sir, that in the hope of destroying a single man, members representing the province of Quebec-in which this society is one of the foremost organizations of its kind, because it has made the French-Canadian name known in all insurance circles throughout the continent of North America-is it possible that in the hope of crushing down a single man, a member should take the risk of injuring the future of an institution'of that kind? This will show, Sir, what is the spirit which animates members who, to flatter their own egotism, to give a chance for the employment of their verbosity and pomposity, would like to be alone in the field; would like to let posterity know that in the year of Our Lord 1921 there was a very big man who represented at the same time the
two separate constituencies of Maissonneuve and Gaspe.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was just concluding my remarks by reading a report from the actuary of the Society of Artisans on the management, from a financial standpoint, of the affairs of that society. I do not want to weary the House with that question, but I would like to put on Hansard the following remarks which will conclude the point that I had been making before six o'clock. This question of the Artisans and this question of Le Club Lafontaine were dealt with in the Courier de St. Hyacinthe, which at the time was a Conservative newspaper in my riding, and following the advice of my friends in the constituency, I instituted legal proceedings agdinst that newspaper. The owners of the newspaper came to me asking for a settlement out of court. This I refused. The matter went to judgment, and the two questions were declared to.be slanders and malicious affirmations against a public man with no good ground for them. The judgment was rendered by His Lordship the late Mr. Justice Charbonneau.
There was another judgment in the same matter of the Artisans before the Superior Court of Montreal presided over by His Lordship Mr. Justice Mercier. The whole question of the investments of the society was looked into, and the judgment declared that there was nothing in those accusations. The plaintiff was not satisfied; he inscribed his case in the Court of Review, and in the last days of 1920 judgment was rendered unanimously confirming the judgment of His Lordship Mr. Justice Mercier. When my former friends decided to take up this question, I wrote on the 29th January last to the headquarters of the society asking the Board of Directors, as much for the sake of the society as for my personal sake to reestablish the facts as they were according to the books. On the 1st February, 1921, the Board of Directors held a meeting at which were present: Mgr. G. M. LePail-lour, general chaplain, Messrs. Napoleon Deschamps, 1st vice-president, General L.

G. Bertrand, Dr. J. E. Raeicot, J. E. C. Daoust, Dr. E. Hurtubise, E. Desjarlais, S. Dupere, general directors; Henri Roy, general secretary-treasurer; Louis Fontaine, assistant general secretary-treasurer; Dr. J. A. Rouleau, chief physician and Zenon Fontaine, legal counsel, under the presidency of Mr. Rudolphe Bedard, general president. This is the motion which was adopted unanimously by the Board of Directors of the society, which motion, in my mind, should do away with all the attacks to which I have been subjected :
The Executive Council, after deliberation, declare:	that the administration of Mr. L. J.
Gauthier has been progressive, wise, prudent and profitable; that the Society recognizes1 with pleasure the important services that have been rendered to it by Mr. Gauthier in his capacity of legislative adviser as well as with his ability in administrative matter. In a word, the society must congratulate itself upon having Mr. Gauthier as one of its directors and as -resident, as1 has been acknowledged by the highest tribunal of the society, the conference heid in 1915. I do not want to take up too much of the time of the House; but I believed, as long as I was a simple member of a political party and these accusations were brought against me by my opponents, I had nothing to complain of; it was their right to try to persuade the electors that I was not worthy of the confidence of my constituents. But my status has changed since last fall, and when my former friends, the Liberals, took upon themselves those accusations which have been declared futile, malicious, and slanderous, I thought it was my duty, equally for my constituents as for my family and myself, and also for the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government (Mr. Meighen) to get clear away from the shadow of these accusations because I have been called to public conferences with the constituted authorities of this Parliament.
What has been my stand all along? Can my former friends, the so-called Liberals of Quebec, complain because I am to-day in favour of protection, as I was in former days in favour of protection? At the last convention of the Liberal party held in the month of August, 1919, in the city of Ottawa, when the time had arrived to choose delegates for that convention, I took pains to go to the manufacturers of my city of St. Hyacinthe and I told them that I was afraid that the Liberal party, with the two factions of Montreal and Quebec, would alter, change and amend the acknow-

ledged policy of the Liberal party. I was afraid that they would ask for a reduction of tariff duties, and I wanted the manufacturers to help me, if that were possible, to have the Liberal party adhere to this platform of protection. During the convention, the authorities of the convention on three different occasions offered to give me an opportunity of addressing it, and I refused because I was not in sympathy with the platform which was prepared at the time, and I thought it was my duty first to remain true to my electors, to my principles and to the principles for which my province has fought since 1878.
On a former occasion, I stated on the floor of this House that the hour of Quebec would strike. The Government supporters thought that there was a threat, a menace in those words. I took pains to state that it was only a declaration. It was not necessary to have the ability of a prophet. Everybody knows that it is impossible to keep in a solid block the minority of a country in public affairs. This marvellous thing has been done once by a man who stood is this country, in the Empire, and especially in his own province, as the idol of his race and the representative of all our aspirations. This has been done once. It cannot be repeated. Where is the man in the ranks of the Liberal party who could go to-day to the province of Quebec and bring back here a solid Quebec block? I should like to be shown that man; but he does not exist. And mind you, Mr. Speaker, when the Quebec population was remaining solid in its principles, awaiting its opportunity it was not necessary to be a prophet to understand that the Government, composed as it is of groups and factions united on a certain principle but divided on other questions, would split one of these days, and that one of the groups or perhaps two would separate themselves from the Government; and that would be the time for the province of Quebec, if it knew how to wait for its hour. Now, Sir, is there anything wrong in that declaration? Nothing at all. It is a simple matter of good political sense, and nothing else.
Nobody can believe that the isolation of Quebec must not be terminated. It is impossible in a country like ours to leave aside a population of pretty nearly three millions out of a total of nine millions. These people must have representation in public affairs. They cannot be ignored for all time to come. Sir, because I hold the principles I have enunciated to the House

from my seat here, I have been attacked as a traitor and a renegade. What crime have I committed? To whom am I responsible? The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) this afternoon was trying to belittle the issue by talking of fish and bribery. The hon. member for Brome ought to know that the man who would be weak enough to allow himself to be bribed could not show his face any more in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Brome should understand, even if he does not respect my belief, that there are situations in this life which require resolution. The hon. member for Brome may think it is all right for himself to represent a constituency of 13,000 souls when according to the last census, the unit of representation was 30,080. The hon. member for Brome should understand that when he speaks from his seat in the House, he speaks not for his own personal benefit, .but for those he represents on the floor of the House. He Speaks for his province, and for the benefit of his country, and, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Brome has that high esteem of himself, can he not respect the beliefs of others who, though they may not be as bright as he, yet are as honest as he is, and who. are entitled to their opinion as long as they are willing to fight for it? No, Sir. The hour of Quebec has struck, I repeat the words.
Why has it struck? Sir, it is the privilege of my province, and to the honour of my race, to have given to this country every time the darkest clouds rose over the horizon a man who was strong enough to command the respect of a majority of this country, and at the same time to command the obedience of the men of my race. In 1840, after the rebellion of 1837 and 1839 Lower and Upper Canada were united under circumstances that were more than dangerous. When, with the population in [DOT]Lower Canada double that of Upper Canada, with a deposit in the chartered banks of Lower Canada and a deficit in the finances of Upper Canada, both provinces were united on an equal footing as to representation and finances, Upper Canada to have half of the money deposited by Lower Canada and Lower Canada to take half the debt of Upper Canada, the Union was looked upon by my people as an insult and they refused to submit to it. Then Louis Hypolyte Lafontaine came into the public arena. He appealed to the majority in the country and appealed to his own people, and the Union Act was passed.
That Act may not have been a success from all points of view, but at all events it created an atmosphere once more of peace, harmony and traquility in this country. Then in 1849, when the annexation memorandum was signed, and when the Parliament buildings in Montreal were burned, when this country was on the verge of disruption, Cartier arose and appealed to the majority and to my people and they united together and peace was restored once more. In 1867, when the time had come for all the provinces in British North America to weld and work together for the expansion of the country, for the prosperity of its population, and for the agrandize-ment of our resources, Cartier was there again fighting night and day to secure the consummation of the British North America Act.
In 1896 when one of the smallest provinces fin this country saw the Federal Government threatening to encroach upon her school system, a man arose from the province of Quebec, a man of my race. This question had been taken from one tribunal to another during six years, and in the campaign of 1896 Laurier, appealing to all races, all creeds, and all provinces, made the statement " This question of the Manitoba schools has been dragging along for six years. Give me power, and in six months peace will be restored." He obtained power, and peace was restored inside of three months.
I do not pretend to be a Lafontaine, a Cartier, or a Laurier. No; my role is more humble and more modest than that, and as my so-called former friends are very fond of precedents I will turn to the world's history and cite a precedent for the stand I am now taking. In the early days of the Christian era, in the deserts of Judea, there was a man who preached the advent of a Saviour. This man was known as the Baptist, and when he was asked whether he himself was the Saviour, he answered that he was not worthy to untie the latchet of that Saviour's shoes; he was only the precursor of the Saviour, who would come to redeem humanity. The Baptist, having fulfilled his mission to the last, was beheaded, but the Saviour came and humanity was redeemed. To-day, Sir, standing in the wilderness of "no man's land," I am, like a Baptist, announcing to this House and to the country that at this time, when every race is hurling insult at the other, when every province is trying to fight every other, when every passion in men's minds is infuriated, a man will come from my province and from my race who will preach

the gospel of toleration and self-respect. He will appeal to the majority of the people of this country and he will show them that though his people constitute the minority, nevertheless there is no reason why the minority and the majority should not unite so that this country will have another era of happiness, of prosperity, of contentment, of good-will to men who love peace and harmony and are proud to live under the protection of the British Crown and our national institutions. I say, this man will come. The hour of Quebec has come, and this man will save the situation.

I desire
at the outset, in common with other members who have spoken, to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address on the excellent way in which they have acquitted themselves. I can hardly, however, concur in all that has been said ljy the hon. gentleman who has just concluded (Mr. Gauthier). It did appear to me that from the first to last he was saying everything he could think of in an uncomplimentary way about the Labour party and the Farmers' party and the Liberal party, which are represented in this House, in I view of the portfolio which he seems so anxious to secure in the future. It comes with bad taste from the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) to ridicule all his former friends in the old Province of Quebec, and in one respect particularly I take exception to his remarks.
I object to the uncomplimentary way in which he referred to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) who was formerly Postmaster General in the Laurier Administration, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that . re-[DOT] presenting as I have the privilege to do, a constituency where a great number of French-Canadian citizens hold the high positions and occupy some of our best farms I was charged personally with the duty of conveying to the hon. member for Gaspe, in his hour of bereavement as a result of his great sacrifice to the cause of the country, in the loss of his son, the sincere sympathy of many of my constituents. When we hear an hon. gentleman ridiculing a citizen who has stood so high in the esteem of the people of this country in the past, I think we may safely assume that many of his words will fall on deaf ears not anly in Quebec but in every other part of the Dominion. In this respect I hope I shall be permitted to read an item or two which appeared in a newspaper in the province of Quebec and which I think will be of in-
terest to the members of this House. 1 quote the following:
Since the opening of Parliament the Hon. Mr. Lemieux occupies the seat immediately next to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier's, and that preferment is merited. A member of Par liament for the last 22 years, Mr. Lemieux by his assiduity, his industry, his correct be haviour, and his thoughtfulness in the fulfil ment of his duties has well earned the -sward of being officially acknowledged as Laurier's first lieutenant in the Province of Quebec.
However, it is on the floor of the House of commmons that the Hon. Mr. Lemieux shows to best advantage. Trained in the best traditions of parliamentary life, holding the tenets of the sound English Liberal faith, in constant sympathy with the views of ail the great men who have contributed by their speeches and their writings to the perfecting of parliamentary practice, he is wholly at ease when ttfking an active part in the various debates.
Could a greater compliment be paid to any Parliamentarian in this country than that contained in :the two extracts I have just read? And they were published in one of the Quebec newspapers which was controlled by the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe, and were his words over his own signature. These were the words of the hon. gentleman in regard to one of our Canadian statesmen, a man who well deserved the compliment. Yet to-night he sees fit to cast aspersion upon him. I will not make any accusations against the hon. gentleman, but we have seen by the press that he had been in communication with the Government with a view to securing a position that would bring him greater benefit than he might obtain as a private member; and because greater statesmen than he might be given a preference over him he gets up in his place and takes up two hours of the time of the House in saying unkind things of his former friends from the province of Quebec in this Parliament and in the local legislature. What confidence can the people of Canada have in the utterances of the hon. gentleman? At his words the ministers of the 'Government might well hold their heads down, from the Minister of Justice to the least among them. There were plaudits from the back-benchers in abundance when such -language was used by the hon. gentleman, but which one of those gentlemen opposite was brave enough to walk over the floor and shake hands with him and congratulate him? His only congratulations were his own handshakes, and he got a very cold reception from all friends whose cause he was pleading. I say that it comes with very bad taste from the hon. member, who recognised the ability of the member for Gaspe,

-a gentleman who sat at the right hand of the late Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Sir, the people of Canada, irrespective of nationality, many of whom were not his political supporters, were admirers of that great British Canadian Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and to-night, on the second anniversary of his death, they mourn his loss. Under such circumstances it is pathetic to think that one who was supposed to be a supporter of Sir Wilfrid and an admirer of the great work that he accomplished in his life time, would lend himself to the task of trying to drive a wedge between- the followers of that lamented statesman for the benefit of men who always did their utmost fo oppose him. I say, Sir, that such conduct on the part of the hon. gentleman exhibits the worst possible taste, and I believe it will have a contemptuous reception in the old province from which that hon. gentleman comes, as well as in the English speaking provinces. To-night I am in the unique position of occupying the same seat as the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe occupied not more than a year ago when that hon. gentleman, undertook to reply to a speech delivered by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat). On that occasion the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe assured the Government that the people of the province of Quebec had received bad treatment. Let me quote his actual words:
Speaking in any own name, and for my province, I will quote tlhe words of one of our public men who says that the province of Quebec is not in a state of mind to enter into any conference ; it has been misjudged; it has been badly treated; it has been slandered ; it is waiting for its hour and 'after that it will confer, but not before.
Waiting for the hour! In the interest of the province of Quebec? No, Sir, in the interest of the hon. member for St. - Hyacinthe himself. He was waiting for the hour to come that would, if possible, give him a better position. It was not the interest of his constituents or the citizens of the old province of Quebec that he was thinking of. He was waiting for an opportunity to get into the Government; but I can assure him, after studying the faces of members of the Cabinet and other hon. gentlemen opposite, that if ever a man crucified himself and sacrificed his chance of getting a high position in public life, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe has done this on the present occasion.
From the hon. gentleman's first remarks it would appear that he had been in consultation with the Prime Minister; he
uttered words and used arguments almost identical with those which the Prime Minister employed. He said that there should not be a general election until after the census had been taken; and he let the cat out of the bag when he said that the city of Montreal, which now has twelve representatives in this House, would, after a redistribution of seats, have twenty. He said that the unit of population would then be forty thousand instead of thirty thousand.
Dollars.

Let me tell the hon. gentleman that the province of Quebec is the pivot of Confederation. It does not make any difference what the unit of population may be, the province of Quebec can only have sixty-five representatives in this Parliament. It is interesting to make a contrast between the remarks of the Prime Minister and those of the hon. gentleman. The Prime Minister, in his flowery and beautiful fashion, declares that we cannot have an election until we give the West its proper representation, and by way of a decoy the figures ten to twenty-five were suggested. But the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe, as I have already said, let the cat out of the bag when he stated that it is to Montreal, Toronto, and the other big-cities of the Dominion that the Government is- anxious to give greater representation.
Let me make a suggestion in this connection. If the Government intends to hang on and not appeal to the country it should, regardless .of the stipulations of the Act of Confederation, start taking the census immediately and not wait until June. In the large cities and towns of Canada there are many men out of employment. In the City of Chatham there are twenty or thirty returned men who are anxious to get work, and these are men that are well, qualified to be employed in the census .taking and would give every satisfaction. I repeat, let the taking of the census be started at the earliest possible date so that the men who are out of employment will be able to get work now when they need it, and not wait until June when there will be no lack of employment. I hope the Government will give some consideration to this thought.
It was also interesting to hear the Prime Minister during his speech make reference to the "ill fated National Transcontinental Railway." Of that enterprise the Prime Minister spoke in the most mournful tones. Let me ask the Government why high

officials of the Canadian National Railways, at a time when fuel throughout the country was most expensive, allowed the ties to be removed from different railway tracks in Canada, piled up in cords and cords and the torch applied to them, instead of placing that fuel at the disposal of people in humble circumstances so as to enable them to keep their homes and their families warm. The Prime Minister may speak of this railway as "ill fated", but I do not think that it would be possible for any enterprise to succeed where such extravagance is practised. If a person were starting out in business he would employ the right class of men to make that business a success, and the same course should be pursued by the Government in regard to the National Railway System. It should employ men of the highest calibre and ability with the necessary knowledge to look after the important interests entrusted to them from time to time. But, Sir, what class of men has the Government been appointing in connection with the National Railway System? We find according to press announcements of July 7th, 1920, that the man who has been appointed to one of the most important positions on the National Railway System, with an elaborately furnished suite of offices in the City of Chicago, is no other person than Mr. DeWitt Foster, who was read out of the Conservative Party by the late Prime Minister, and sent back to his constituency, on account of the way he handled matters in connection with the purchase of horses for the Government during the late great war. That gentleman's management of affairs was so scandalous, it was so ridiculous and farcical, that it involved an expense of thousands and thousands of dollars to the people of Canada.
Yet, Sir, this man is sent to the city of Chicago to occupy one of the most important positions in connection with the Canadian National Railways. Is it any wonder that we hear my right hon. friend the Prime Minister speaking of the "ill-fated" National Transcontinental road when men of the type I have referred to are associated with our national railway system? How can you expect that system to be a success, how can you expect not to have deficits, when such men are on the staff? Last year the deficit amounted to $47,000,000, this year it is estimated that it will reach $65,000,000.
What does it mean? It means that we must expect a continuance of deficits if such things as I am about to bring to the

attention of the House are typical. I am informed that the most important train leaving the city of Toronto, instead of being filled with passengers who had paid their fares, was composed of special cars for the benefit of a few friends of the Government. The would-be passengers who were prepared to pay had to cross over to the ticket office of the competing road and buy tickets for Ottawa. Then I am advised on very reliable authority-and the Government can ascertain whether my information is correct or not-that the trains running from Vancouver to Toronto on the days before Christmas were loaded to capacity, but fifty per cent of the passengers were travelling on passes. If this be untrue, no person will be more pleased than myself, because if half of those passengers were travelling on passes, it goes to show why to some extent the people who are trying to ship their products are being held up by the higher freight rates now being charged; and the necessity of higher freight rates is no doubt because the passenger trains are not paying. In view of this condition pf affairs, it seems to me incumbent upon the Government to appoint a committee of this House to deal with the statements which I have brought to their attention. If the Government have the interests of the country at heart, I am confident an investigation will be held.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) may smile, but this is too important a question for him or any other leading member of the Cabinet to smile at. An investigation of the conductors' books will show whether the statement I have made is well founded or not. If it is not correct, all well and good; but if fifty per cent of the passengers at that season of the year were travelling on passes, it is important that the country should know it and that the practice should be promptly discontinued, as our National railways need all the revenue that they san possibly secure to reduce their operating deficits.
Now, Sir, let me go a step further. We have to-day advised the Government to appeal to the people, or place their resignations in the hands of the Governor General so that he may call upon other persons to form a Government which will meet with the endorsation of the country. The right hon. the Prime Minister will probably think that our advice does not count for very much, but let me assure him that the advice we are tendering him now is just as sound as the advice which we proffered

when his Government were about to establish the Board of Commerce. We told them then that the appointment of such a board would be a detriment to the country and would be barren of results. What followed on the appointment of that board has confirmed the soundness of our advice. It will be remembered that the members of that board sat for months, drawing thousands of dollars in salaries and expenses, but not one profiteer was ever put in jail, nor one dollar added to the Treasury as a result of their efforts to put a stop to profiteering.
What we contended then and what we contend now is that we should have a public prosecutor appointed to take action against profiteers. We have complaints, particularly from our returned men, that profiteering still continues. For instance, notwithstanding that hides are to-day cheaper than they have been for years, those men complain that their children's shoes cost the same price as when the war was raging. We hear |rom the farmers that they are getting only $13.50 a hundred for their hogs, and yet to-day bacon is twenty cents a pound dearer in Canada than in England. These two cases alone are sufficient to justify an investigation.
If we are going to allow these combines to exist, we cannot expect to attract as many people to assist us in agriculture as we need to-day. I have been informed that in the case of Peterson versus the Dominion Tobacco Company, tried at Sandwich in December, 1919, before Mr. Justice Middleton, there was filed as an exhibit a telegram from the representative of the companies in the Tobacco Buyers' Association to the Macdonald company of Montreal, who were not members of the association, asking them, in effect, to come in and agree to keep the price down; and that Stewart, of the Macdonald company, swore in evidence that his company was asked to agree with the other companies not to pay more in 1919 than thirty cents per pound. This, Sir, went to show that there was an attempt to combine against the producers of tobacco in the counties of Kent and Essex, which meant that the men who returned from overseas and took up tobacco growing had their tobacco hanging in their barns with no chance of selling, it. This year there has been a tremendous tobacco crop and from the absence of buyers the farmers suspect a combine has been formed to force down prices, to the detriment of the growers. Is it not worth while for the Government to take
this matter up, for it will be remembered that the men who went overseas were promised that combines would not be allowed, and those men naturally expect to have that promise redeemed.
To-day, Sir, we are trying to get men to locate upon the land. And what do we find? We find that the agricultural implement manufacturing companies, not only the Massey Harris Company, but the International Harvester Company, the Cock-shutt Company and all the other big implement concerns, have raised the price of binders $30 over last year's price, which was the highest on record. How Sir, can we expect to induce men to locate upon the farms if we allow these implement concerns to extract such exorbitant prices from those who have to use these implements? Last year it took 250 bushels of oats to buy a binder; to-day it takes 700 bushels. I find that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) is, going to follow me. If that is the case I ask him to challenge the statement that I have made. The same thing applies on other agricultural machinery all down the line. This is a matter that should receive some consideration at the hands of the Government.
In conclusion, I have only this to say, that if at the next general election the Government expect to be returned with anything like a respectable following, the matters which I have brought to the attention of the House will have to be given greater consideration than they have received in the past.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne always covers a very wide field. A number of interesting subjects are mentioned in the Speech itself, but it is not necessary that one should confine himself to those particular subjects; a general latitude is permissible on the part of one who addresses the House on this occasion.
But before taking up the matters to which I wish to refer in connection with the Address, I want to say a word with regard to our new Prime Minister. It is the first opportunity that I have had of speaking in the House since the right hon. gentleman was elevate to the high position he now occupies. I have followed his career for a number of years: He came from that part of the country in which I have the honour to live,-and that does not make him any the worse. He combines

the steadfastness, carefulness and shrewdness of the East with the push and progress of the West, and that combination should go to make a man of breadth and of enterprise, a man eminently fitted to fill the high position to which my right hon. friend has been called. So far as I am concerned, though I am an independent man in some ways, I profess to give my allegiance to the Prime Minister so far as I can see my way to do it-whenever he brings forward measures that I believe to be in the general interests of the country. I do not think, from what I know of him that he will bring forward many measures, either now or at any time, that are not in the general interests of the people. I wish, therefore, that the tenure of office of the right hon. gentleman as the Prime Minister of Canada may be a long and successful one.
We have had a rather interesting exhibition this afternoon. There has been more or less of a family fight; and of course that is always "pie" to us if it occurs on the other side.
One-sided.

I can quite imagine that some of the remarks of the member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) were not very much relished by gentlemen opposite. It was really a study to sit here and watch the varrying shades of contempt and disgust that occasionally played upon the features of hon. gentlemen on the other side.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), the gentleman with the loud voice and the small constituency, came in for a fair share of the speaker's attention. I have always thought that the member for Brome, if he kept on long enough, would make a convert of some kind, and apparently he succeeded this afternoon, because his eloquent remarks on free trade and various other things so incensed the member for St. Hyacinthe that he could hold his seat no longer, and the result was the exhibition that we had of a family squabble. I am sorry that the hon. member for Brome could not see what was coming. He has been trying for this for a long time, and finally his chickens have come home to roost, and he has made a convert. However, it was a kind of backfire business that he did not expect; it has hit the preacher so that he is really in a worse position than the man who was supposed to be the sinner.

The member for Kent, (Ont.) (Mr. McCoig) has attempted to belittle what the member for St. Hyacinthe said. But when the papers come out to-morrow and the speeches of the two hon. gentlemen are read, it will be found that the speech of the member for St. Hyacinthe has created an impression of a very different nature, from that created by any remarks of the member for Kent. Whatever may be said with regard to the right or the wrong of the situation, as the member for St. Hyacinthe sees it, there is no doubt that he spoke from a full heart and with a conscientious desire to do what he conceived to be a very difficult, and perhaps, a somewhat dangerous duty to his fellow-men, especially with regard to the Province of Quebec. I give him all cred for having made one of the most impressive speeches from the province of Quebec that I have heard in a good many days. If a few more of our friends across the way will study questions of the day in the same light as the member for St. Hyacinthe has done we shall have a rapprochement between the old Provinces of Ontario and Quebec the like of which has not been seen for many years. That would be a very desirable consummation indeed, and for my part I hold out both hands to my hon. friend.
The member for Brome took great exception to the Prime Minister possibly opening a little seat on this side for one or two repentant gentlemen from the other side, but almost in the same breath he said he welcomed from this side the member from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) who was expected shortly to take his seat on the Opposition benches. The inconsistency of the member for Brome was certainly remarkable when he could make a bid for the member for Halifax to cross the floor and occupy a front bench-which is nearly a Cabinet position, because no doubt all the members of the new Cabinet made up from members on the other side when they came in will be named by the member for Brome. The member for Halifax, therefore, might consider himself as good as a cabinet minister. But
9 p.m. having said this, why should the member for Brome be offended if the Prime Minister should say that he would welcome gentlemen from the other side? It has long been the desire of Ontario men to have representatives from the province of Quebec sitting on this side as they used to. We can sit here more comfortably with them alongside of us than we can simply as a number of Ontario men

sitting together. In the old days the good old Conservative party had the backing of the French-Canadians to a great extent- in fact, the backbone of Sir John Macdonald's party on many occasions were the representatives from the province of Quebec, and it seems to me they had quite as much light in those days as we have in these.
There are many respects in which the provinces of Quebec and Ontario are alike. Quebec is a manufacturing centre; so is Ontario, and at such a time as this I take off my hat to Quebec as being probably the mpst stable labour province in Canada to-day. Quebec has shown itself during the last two or three years to be a province with a great deal of self-respect and a great deal of backbone, and one that is doing more, perhaps, in the reconstruction period following the Great War than any other province of our Dominion. While we, in Ontario, and our brethren too, in the West, are giving way to all kinds of fad legislation and calling for every conceivable kind of government, Quebec sticks to the old rule, maintains the old stand, attends to her own knitting, keeps her factories running-supplied by the labour, the brawn and the brain of the good inhabitants of that province. I give them credit, then, for playing at this time a very important part in the re-establishment of Canada after the war.
Now, having said this much I do not wish to enter into a further discussion of the family affairs of my hon. friends opposite. Before touching, however, upon some of the items specifically dealt with in the Speech from the Throne, I feel that I must pay some little attention to one or two remarks made by my friend from Kent (Mr. McCoig). I understand that he comes from a tobacco district. I do not know whether he himself smokes much of the tobacco grown there, but if he does perhaps that, would be a higher recommendation of it than we would otherwise have. I understand that the tobacco growers in his constituency have recently asked that the modest duty of one dollar a pound be placed upon tobacco. What percentage that would be I must leave the hon. member for Kent to calculate. So far as I know the price of tobacco in the western section, it runs from twenty-five up to forty-five cents per pound. Therefore, a modest duty of one dollar per pound on this would sound fairly big as a percentage, being somewhere between two and three hundred per cent. My hon.
friend has taken occasion, as he often does, to allude to the firm which bears my name, but with the management of which I have no connection. He informs the House and the country that we have raised the price of our binders twenty or thirty per cent. If he knows the firm as well as he ought to know it, because it is no secret that the hon. gentleman was at one time an agent for the company which he is so glad to abuse on various occasions, he knows they manufacture no mowers and no binders and never have done so.
You handle the Frost & Wood mowers and binders in western Ontario.

The handling of them is one thing and the manufacture is quite another. It is true we take orders for and sell those implements, but not a single one is manufactured by the firm, and the hon. gentleman knows that perfectly well; so that when he speaks of the Cockshutt firm raising the prices of those implements, he knows he is making a misrepresentation because they have nothing at all to do with the manufacture of those machines. Further, as a practical farmer, as I presume he is, he knows that during the war, during the last five years, any farmer either in eastern or western Canada going to any market in this country with a load of produce, whether it were pork, beans, wheat, oats, barley or rye or any of the products of the farm, could take back, as a result of the sale of that load, as many implements as he ever did before the war. I do not think that can be said of everything, but it can be said of the implement business, and of all industries in Canada none, perhaps, suffered more than, did that same implement business. I do not, however, want to speak of that. The time will come later in the session when we can take care of that, but I do not like my hon. friend who was carried away by his feelings-and possibly he had some good excuse because he was smarting, under the remarks of the hon. mepiber for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier)-to make such sweeping statements as he did. But we know that as regards the products of his constituency, which are sugar beets, corn and all those items, he is very careful not to advocate any policy that would bring any less to the growers of any of those products than they have received in the past. How he can pose as a free trader -and I am not quite sure whether he does

so entirely-when he has two or three sugar factories and several other large industries in his riding, I can hardly understand; nor can I understand how he can advocate that all barriers should be removed and at the same time retain those in his county. I must apologize for having spent so much time upon the hon. member for Kent (Mr. MeCoig) because I am not sure that his remarks deserve it.
I want, before going further, to refer to the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who I am sorry is not in the chamber. I am not going to spend many moments upon his amendment, but I desire to point out to him one or two things in connection with it. In the first place I hold in my hand the Brantford Expositor, which is well known as one of the staunch Liberal papers of Ontario and of Canada, and this is what it has to say with regard to the point at issue:
If the Hon. Arthur Meighen holds the reigns of power long enough to pass the new Redistribution Bill based on the census taken this year and frankly implements the obligation to secure an equitable representation by population and then appeals to the country, he will pursue a wise course of statesmanship and one hard to successfully challenge.
I recommend those remarks to my hon. friend who moved this amendment. He says that this Government has no mandate. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) pointed out several mandates which this Government had, and that the Opposition were ready to acknowledge that the Government had the mandate when they raised the indemnity last session and my hon. friends pocketed it. My hon. friends say nothing about that. This Government only about three years ago was elected by the largest majority of both members and popular vote of any Government that I have ever known of in Canada.
Where are they now?

There are many of
them here as my hon. friend will find out, and they are here to stay for quite a little while in spite of the efforts of the hon. member of Pontiac to dislodge them. I suppose he would carry them out on railway trains if he had the opportunity, as he is a great railway expert, but I do not want to be diverted from this matter by the hon. gentleman. This Government wa^ elected by the largest majority of the popular vote that any Government ever received in Canada. That cannot be successfully contradicted. Therefore, they

had the mandate from the people to occupy the treasury benches not only for the duration of the war, but for five years, in spite of anything that may be said to the contrary. I knew something about this fight up in our section: I had a little to do with it, and I never once heard the question raised as to the right of the Government to retain power so long as the Parliamentary term was not exceeded and, as well known, that term was to be five years.
My hon. friend complains that this mandate does not exist now, although it has run only about three years. Let me point out to him the inconsistency of himself and many of his friends in this regard. * We have to-day in two of the provinces at least, in Manitoba and in Ontario, Governments sitting that have not now and never had any mandate from the people. The Ontario Government polled only about one-third of the vote. The Premier of Ontario was unheard of on the platform throughout the election; he was not even a candidate, and the Farmers' Party and the Labour Party between them polled only about one-third of the votes that were polled in the recent election in Ontario. Still, my hon. friend does not question their mandate. Oh no, they are good for it. Why? Because he considers they are his friends; he says that there is little difference between them. Well, I am sorry for the farmers if there is little difference between the leader of the Opposition and his followers and the following of the Agrarian party. But there is the fact that the Government in Ontario to-day, sitting there and legislating for this great province, are there by reason of about one-third of the provincial vote cast in the recent election. It is true they are largely farmers and they possibly do not recognize that a citizen living in a city has a right to value his vote as highly as a man on the farm, because in Ontario, in the city of Toronto for instance, it takes the vote of three men to offset the vote of one man on the farm.
Is the present Government responsible for that?
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear." The chances are, if the statement of my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) is true, that my hon. friend from Brome may find that his little constituency has disappeared from the map after re-distribution, and holding the views he does, I question very much if he could get a seat in Montreal where the people have some intelligence on economic questions. My hon. friend from Brome represents, I believe the smallest body of citizens in the Dominion of Canada that are in one hive, some 13,000 people. That means that Montreal, the city of intelligence in the province of Quebec, the city of big men and big things, requires from 60,000 to 70,000 votes to offset the vote of 13,000 people in the little county of Brome. Oh, my, that is a beautiful little county. I am somewhat surprised that a gentleman coming from so small a place should develop such a pugnacious tendency as my hon. friend has. He certainly had broadened out beyond the confines of his constituency. To hear him lay down the law, not only on free trade and protection, but all the rest of it, you would think he was the oracle of the province of Quebec, but after hearing the opinion the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville holds of him I have been forced to a different conclusion. My hon. friend certainly thought he would put the Premier in a very bad hole to-day when he pointed his finger at him and dared him to offer a bait to any of the gentlemen sitting around my hon. friend. Has my hon. friend any misgivings in his heart that the Premier even of the Dominion of Canada could tempt any of those just men to cross the floor under any condition whatsoever? I cannot imagine how my hon. friend could think the Premier had sufficient to offer of the loaves and fishes. After hearing the hon. member for Brome speak you would think you could take him up to the top of the mountains here, the Laurentians that the hon. gentleman knows so well, and offer him all the Kingdom he could survey from there, all that glory, if only he would cross the floor, but never conceive of him coming across.
I hope not.

No, he could not be tempted. But the hon. gentleman, apparently, having seen the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville go away from him

down into No Man's land, is afraid that the offers of the Prime Minister may win over some of the gentlemen around him. I must admitthat this microbe of protection is very catching. It has got into the heart of my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Rouville in spite of my hon. friend from Brome, and it is liable to break out yet in unexpected places. I imagined I saw a wave of unrest this afternoon move over the features of some of my friends the Agrarians opposite, when they found the plague of protection had got into the very next row to them. However, that will no doubt disappear. We know these gentlemen are studying economics, because they have told us so. I wonder if they could also tell us that they study economy as well. I have not found much evidence of that.
The luxury tax has made us study economy.

That is the kind of economy the farmer is practising in Ontario. He is not practising economy with the public monies. I was going to point out to my hon. friends that in the province of Ontario the so-called Agrarian Government has the biggest expenditure ever, and when you find fault they say: Wait till you see us next year. The expenditure in the province of Ontario under this new combination runs close up to $75,000,000 for the past year, a sum vastly in excess of the requirements of this House when I first came into it a few years ago.
Mr. JOHN A. MAHARG (Maple Creek) : How much of that expenditure was on capital account?

I am quite ready to tell my hon. friend if he gives me time. I am pointing out that the total expenditure of the new Government in Ontario, which had economy as one of the planks in their platform, lexceeds that of any previous government by about $25,000,000. I think it is that much greater than the expenditure in the previous year under the late government, and that is only little compared with what they intend to do. They say, like Mr. Tarte said at one time: Wait till you see us next year. The expenditure that we are confronted with in the province of Ontario at the present time under the new order of things will stagger the people of this old province, especially the tax-payers. They will have to pay pretty dearly for the experiment of a group government and a new order of things in the province of Ontario. In reply to my

hon. friend from Maple Creek, whose question was a very fair one, I understand that the expenditure on current account runs between $22,000,000 and $23,000,000, and that the expenditure on capital account is pretty nearly $50,000,000. My hon. friend will probably know whether that is correct or not, but I understand that is about how the figures stand. Then new taxes are proposed, five or six in number, only one of which will slightly touch the farmer. All . the rest will go to the city people. That is how the farmers are showing their favour to the cities, by giving them five times as much to pay in taxation as they pay themselves.
Now, they went in with a flourish of trumpets with regard to economy, and when our hon. friends opposite come into power, as they expect to do in the near future in this Dominion, in addition to the said economics which we have been assured they are studying, they will also have to study economy, or we shall find the expense of the Dominion jumping up in the same proportion that we in the province of Ontario are confronted with at the present time.

Is the hon.
gentleman aware that he is in Ottawa and not in Toronto?

It is very kind of my hon. friend to remind me of that faet. We are told by the hon. Mr. Drury that he is only occupying his position in Ontario temporarily, that he expects to give the economic situation at Ottawa his early attention, and therefore we are justified in connecting Toronto with Ottawa in that respect, because our friends, though new on the job, are very ambitious and I can tell you they are excellent spenders. They not only spend money lavishly, but they spend, according to the doctrines laid down by some of our friends from the West, a large part of the money on the other side of the line; and then we wonder why the Canadian dollar is shrinking and ever shrinking, and why it takes $1.15 or $1.20 to pay for a dollar's worth of goods. It is because of the policy that my hon. friends would thrust upon this country, by which they would increase still further what is already far too large, that is to say, purchases from the United States. One would think that the legislation now proposed at Washington, and which we are told the Senate yesterday passed, would give a little new light to my hon. friends opposite. What about the

Fordney Bill? Have they heard about it? Has my hon. friend from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) realized that the Fordney tariff proposes a duty of 30 cents a bushel on wheat-
Forty cents.

Yes, forty cents on wheat, j20 per cent on flour, 15 cents a bushel on barley and all along the line; on cattle 3 cents per pound, and all the rest of it. Still we find that some of our hon. friends are ready to advocate that in spite of all this treatment which we have received or are about to receive from our neighbors to the south of us, they would continue not only the present liberal policy that has been pursued towards the United States but would increase the advantage still further by a large reduction of duties. So tha to-day the minister in Toronto, Mr. Smith, I think, who brought down the budget, complains that during the past year he has lost $800,000 on the exchange situation alone. Why did he deal so much in the United States? Why did he buy to such an extent in the United States as to incur an additional debt of $800,000 in the province of Ontario on exchange alone? Let the Hon. Mr. Biggs tell him why and how. When he wants road rollers or machinery for his roads does he buy them in Canada? I live close to the neighbourhood where a good deal of money was spent, not to much advantage, J am sorry to say, and along that road you can see evidences of where he buys rollers. It is plainly marked on the implements themselves showing that they come from the United States, and our dollar is going steadily down. I am glad to know that this Government proposes, in the light of the investigation that has taken place, to try to remedy some of these difficulties by giving a tariff that will be more safe and sound for the industries of Canada, and that will restore to its rightful place the value of the Canadian dollar. I believe there is -no better dollar in the world than the Canadian dollar. We have resources in Canada that make our money just as good as any in the world, and therefore it is penalizing us in a way that should not be permitted in this country that we should buy $2 worth of goods in the United States for every $1 we sell them, and that has been the fact within the last two or three years. We have bought $2 for every $1 sold them. My policy is to buy less and sell more in the United States and thus restore the balance
which has so far gone against us. That is a safe and sound policy and I recommend it to my hon. friends. I do not want to be hard on my Agrarian friends over the way. I am glad to see a good body of them here, and I think it is a pity sometimes, when I see them kept here all day long and late at night, that the rosy complexions and rotund figures of some of our swarthy brethren from the soil should he depleted, so to speak, by having to attend to public business in the House of Commons. Of course, I am somewhat interested in not wishing to see the group grow too rapidly. The hon. member for Maple Creek, in spite of his heterodox notions on some matters of business and public policy, looks like a man who has a good conscience, in the ruddy complexion and youthful appearance he shows in the House of Commons. I congratulate my hon. friend that in spite of all the strenuous efforts he has put forth in the interests of the Agrarian party he is looking so very hearty as I see him to-night.	-
I did not intend to dwell for more than a few moments on the tariff, and I have said already more than I intended to say on that question. Before I resume my seat I wish to direct attention to two or three matters on which possibly I may not be quite in line with some 'of my colleagues on this side of the House. I said, in the first place, when paying my tribute of respect to the new Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen), that I intended to follow him on all possible occasions. But I must say, as I have said on previous occasions, that in so far as the much-vaunted League of Nations is concerned, I am still a doubter. I am sorry to have to make that declaration, but I am glad to know that there must be either in the mind of His Excellency or in those of some of his advisers, somewhat the same opinion as I have myself with regard to the League of Nations, because I find, in the fifth line of the clause dealing with that subject, that it is termed a "great experiment." Truly, a great experiment, Mr. Speaker. I was very much interested and very much enlightened by the address of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) yesterday in dealing with that matter. He gave us some very enlightening information with regard to the aims of this great League of Nations that has been formed. I could have hoped that he would have dwelt not only upon what appeared to be the sunny side of the League, but on a few other mat-



ters that have perplexed and bewildered us and caused us some regret. For instance, what about disarmament? I understand that that question was shelved. Again, for example, what about reparations? What about indemnities? It is true that the hon. gentleman in speaking on this subject told us that they were going to cut across the history of six thousand years and reverse the old order of things. It has always been the order of things in the past that to the victors in war belong the spoils. It may be a false doctrine, but it has always existed, and it seems to me that in making peace, if we have won the war we have lost the peace, or some of the pieces at least. It may be a false doctrine but it was always there; and it seems to me that in making the peace if we won the war we have lost the peace, or we have lost some of the pieces. What about making Germany pay?
Some hon. GENTLEMEN: Hear, hear.

We in Canada are
to be bled hard for a generation to pay for the cost of this great war. Do we forgive the Germans their debt? Do we say that after bringing that terrible ruin upon this world, after bringing ruin to a large part of France and turning nine millions of people out of their homes, and after devastating Belgium, Roumania, Serbia, and all those countries of Europe, that our delegates shall come back without any proposal with regard to what we are going to make Germany pay? Because that is one of the very few arguments that a German understands. He does understand though when you tap him in the pocket; it is one of the most sensitive parts of his constitution. I would like the Minister of Justice and the late President of the Privy Council to deal still further with this matter, and I believe they will do so. I should like them to take up one or two of these knotty points, and tell us what they are going to make Germany do with regard to reparation to France, to Belgium, and to those devastated countries, and tell us whether there is any possibility of Canada receiving some slight share of the immense indemnity that should be paid by reason of her financial sacrifice. Talk about taxation! I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is being taxed in a way that we have never known before. That is the case, and yet some of our agrarian friends say, "Put on an income tax." I have had the privilege of paying two income taxes, one to the Dominion Government and one to the local muni-

cipality, within the last six months. I expect to have to pay another before the year is out, making three within a year. I tell you that many of our people are feeling this taxation and feeling it keenly, and in all fairness I say to the Ministry, and especially to the' Minister of Finance, that you cannot keep the wheels of commerce going in this country if you are going to take all the profits and a good deal of the capital. Because you have got to pay whether you make money or not. They will allow you to pay on those things on which you make a profit, but if you make a loss you must not take that into consideration -that is not in the bargain. I am glad to notice, Mr. Speaker, that the Government proposes to revise the Income Tax Act. I am glad to know that, because I think it is a wise announcement which will be received with satisfaction by the country. I do not believe that this Government, or any government, desires to take wrongfully from a man anything that he possesses. As I understand it, a government sets the standard of business morality for the country in which it rules-I thing that is a fair proposition-and that no act should be done, either by a strong government or any kind of a government, that would be opposed to justice and would not bear the light of investigation as an honest transaction. I feel that in the hurry of last session there was put through in the Income Tax Bill some of the most iniquitous features that I have ever seen in any legislation. I make these remarks in order that our friends on this side may take notice and during this session rectify what I believe is a grievous wrong. The Income Tax Act makes you your own assessor. You have got to assess yourself, they are not going to give you your bill any more. Formerly the bill was sent in by the man who was going to collect it, but not now. It is going.to be made up by yourself, and you are warned that if you make a mistake of ten per cent you will be fined at that rate on the mistake you made. If you make a twenty per cent mistake you will be fined half the amount of the capital concerned; and if you make a mistake of over twenty per cent woe betide you, because you will be liable to a fine of $10,000 and to six months' imprisonment. Now in all justice I say, Mr. Speaker, that such a state of things as that should be rectified in this Dominion. I am glad to know that such a proposal is on the agenda, and before the session is over we will possibly have that rectified.

Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two with regard to another matter. There are quite a few in Canada who are ready to pull down everything that has been built up with the greatest pains for a thousand years past. I mean in Britain, and in Canada, our laws and a large part of our constitutions are copied from Britain. These persons are prepared to sacrifice all that has been built up at such pains for some current fad that has never been tried out and which is not likely to succeed. That should not obtain with such a people as we have in this Dominion. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that it is the part of good citizenship at the present time to play safe, to advocate no change but what will be for the better; and if you are not absolutely sure that it will be for the better, stick to what you have until you know. If this country, and if civilization itself, is to be saved, there must be more care taken by public men and by those who guide public thought than has been witnessed in Canada in the past. During the past two or three years we have had every kind of heterodox preaching from every soap box that could be found in the province of Ontario. We have it in Ontario and it extends to many of the other provinces both East and West. This is a state of things that should not exist, and I rejoice that our good old friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) has a resolution on the Order Paper, that is to come up a little later in the session, in which he deals with Empire matters. This is no time, Mr. Speaker, to cut the old flag down, to tear apart the few remaining threads that hold Canada to the Mother land. We have but four of them remaining and yet right here in the city of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario and in the heart of the Dominion, we have had it recommended recently by one high in authority that the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council should be done away with, and that the Governor General should no longer come from overseas but should be appointed in Canada.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Brome, who is ready to be carried about by every wind of doctrine and every fad that comes down the line, says "Hear, hear" to the former statement. I wonder if my hon. friend would not call for the Queen of Sheba to come back and rule if it were possible to get her here.

No petticoat
Government.

My hon. friend is
ready to call for anything rather than what he is getting. He is getting a very fair government, why not keep it? Why should we, I say, wish for a moment to cut loose these few remaining threads that bind Canada to the Motherland? Let me tell you what these threads are, as I can see them to be. There is the King-long live the King! There is the flag-long wave the flag! There is the appeal to the Privy Council-long may it continue! Because that appeal has stood between us and a great many very difficult disputes in the past. If time would permit me I could point out where, in respect to the province of Ontario in the past, Sir John Macdonald and Sir Oliver Mowat-a name that was known throughout the length and breadth of the province at that time-had a life and death struggle about an increase of territory. Sir John said "Not one acre of land, not one stick of timber will you get." Sir Oliver Mowat on the other hand said "We will have both." The dispute was carried to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and although I was against Sir Oliver and in favor 6f Sir John I must say that I did not shed any tears when the Privy Council said "Sir Oliver is right on this occasion and Ontario gets both the acres and the timber." [DOT] There is just one case of the value of ar, appeal when a difficulty arises between a province and the Dominion. What could be better than this appeal? And yet we have a man, high in authority in the province of Ontario, who has advocated in Ottawa within recent days that this right of appeal should be done away with. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is no time to tear down any of the safeguards that surround our constitution. The world is full of unrest; tfie Mother Country is beset with troubles and cares, both from without and within; the nation is in peril to-day -Lloyd George tells us so. Will we in Canada, who have practically no grievance, give it out to the world that we, too, are full of unrest and want to cut the painter? Are we going to have an election, as they have had in South Africa recently, to decide whether or not we will stay with the Motherland? I hope not. But, Mr. Speaker, we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that the enemies of the Empire are abroad, they are sowing the seeds of discord wherever they can be sown, and the attempt is being made even in some parts of Canada to raise the red flag and to call not only for the dissolution of the British

Empire, but for the overthrow of constituted Government in this and other parts of the Empire.
In a time such as this none of us who wish well to our country and to our Empire can afford to experiment in any degree with any of those ties that have held us so long to that good old land over the sea. I, for one, trust that I shall not live to see the day when the few remaining threads that hold us to the Motherland from which many of us come will be cut asunder, because bad as may be the example of some ,Britishers, and bad as the rule may be said to be in some parts of the Empire, the world has yet to show any better constitution, any greater safeguards to our liberties, to our rights and to our religious freedom than has been brought to us by reason of the benign rule that has been handed out to the Dominions from over the seas in a very mild way; and we have had not only all, but much more liberty than is enjoyed in most of the countries of the world.
This then in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, is no time to advocate any of those changes that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Me-Master) would so lightly adopt overnight and repent of on the morrow, because I am sure he would repent when he saw the evil he had done; but once he cuts the painter and casts off, he will find no place of repentance, though he should seek it in tears. I beseech him to be a little more guarded when he applauds every fad that comes down the line and is prepared to adopt almost anything in the way of legislation that will bring a change-especially a change of Government. The hon. gentleman does not recognize a good Government when he sees one.
We have not seen one for a long time.

It is the kind of glasses he wears with the result that he cannot see the qualities possessed by the Government that occupies the treasury benches at the present time.
But I hope, Mr. Speaker, whether the appeal to the people come early or whether it be delayed, that the electorate will recognize that we have about as good a form of government-I am not speaking of this particular Government-as exists in any country in the world, and that no attempt will be made in such times as these to upset the apple-cart, to change any of the vital parts of our constitution by the introduction of fads. I see my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) smiling; he

has the referendum and the recall in his mind; I call those fads which we do not want to adopt in this country. I hope that when the appeal comes, whether the party opposite to me or the party on this side or the Agrarian party should succeed to power-and there is quite a possibility that my agrarian friends will he found in the majority, for elections are very uncertain-
They are very uncertain.

I am glad that my hon. friend from Red Deer agrees with me that elections are very uncertain. I believe that if he agrees with me to that extent he is going to vote about the same way as I am on this amendment, because it is safer to hang on to a seat that you are sure of for one year than it is to take the chance of a seat for five years which may not eventuate. I think my hon. friend, who in the absence of the real leader is leading the Agrarian party, is a man on whose judgment I can rely in this respect, and I feel that my words have not been in vain when I get corroboration from the hon. member that he thinks that axiom which I have just pronounced is a true one. I hope he will act on it; and as some of his followers are comparatively new in the House, if he instructs them that he thinks the best interests of the Agrarian party would be served on the present occasion by voting against the amendment and in favour of the continuance of this Government until the census has been taken and redistribution made, I think he will carry conviction to his own constituents and to the people generally in the great provinces in the West, j
I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for thus far trespassing upon the patience of the House. I feel that I have not done anything like justice to the various questions mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, but at the same time I feel that I was justified in making these few remarks, and I hope that the hon. member who has moved the amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King), although he has not heard them, will read them before he casts his vote, and will realize that he will be inconsistent in pushing that amendment now after what I have pointed out is going on in the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, allow me in the time-honoured fashion to congratulate the mover and

seconder of the Address. Though one belongs to the older generation of parliamentarians and the other to the new, they have both worthily fulfilled the task entrusted to them. It is to their credit that they discharged so well the somewhat thankless and politically unprofitable task of bolstering up a dying party. The compliments which they addressed to the ministry and to the Government I cap make no objection to, for I agree fully with the old saying-de mortuis nil nisi bonum.
In reference to the other speakers, We have had two who have given us highly instructive and entertaining addresses on the League of Nations. One, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) seems to be strongly in favour of this grand institution; and the other, the hon. member who has just at down (Mr. Cockshutt), would appear to be rather violently oposed to it. I am sorry, for I hardly think that the opinions either of the Minister of Trade and Commerce or of the hon. member for Brantford will influence in the slightest degree the statesmen of the world who have founded the League.	.
We had another address this afternoon

or, rather, a performance-and I wish to make but a slight reference to it. 1 can only hope that whe.n the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) crosses the floor of the House he will be as true and faithful to his new friendships and to his new friend as he was to the old. I can only hope and pray that he will be as worthy of the trust and confidence of hon. members opposite as he has shown himself to-day to be worthy of our trust and confidence.
I congratulate the new leader of the new party which is now facing us, but not upon the party which he has acquired, the very weakness of which must cause him many a wakeful night. I hope for his sake that he will give the people the chance to deprive him of his friends and so enable him to return to his normal state of mind. I congratulate him, but not on being the choice from such a field; I give him credit for being worthy of better rivals. Nor do 1 congratulate him on the colleagues whom he has inherited; were I to say too much about that I might be accused of sarcasm in vaunting his legacy. But I do congratulate him from the bottom of my heart on having attained the highest position in the gift of the Canadian people. My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe)
corrects me-the highest position in the gift of his Tory friends. Fortune may have favoured him in eliminating from the field other more popular and, perhaps, worthier rivals. It may have favoured him too, in that those members of his Cabinet and those of his colleagues who were not quite certain that he would make the best Prime Minister were unable to put before their followers and before the Tory party one who was better fitted for the position than himself. However, we must say this for him; that his elevation is due, to a large extent, to his own untiring energy, to his own perseverance, to his own courage, and to his undoubtedly high talent. We are quite willing to acknowledge those talents. We are quite willing, from having felt them, to admit the weight and temper of his blows. We are willing to admit also that time and again he has been called upon to save the threatened citadel of Toryism and that time and again he has given unsparingly his learning, his wit and his eloquence to his party. We have only one criticism to make of him: that we consider it would have been far better for the country as a whole had this wit and energy and these high talents been devoted more to the general welfare of the country than to the welfare of a section thereof.
We consider also-and I wonder whether the hon. gentleman was not himself thinking of it yesterday-that the country expects a somewhat greater degree of dignity and of poise in its Prime Minister than is shown by the employment of the tactics of a partisan and the adoption of the policy of a guerilla leader.
