The day before yesterday I noticed that in his remarks there was missing the old fire, the old biting sarcasm, and the result probably was that his speech lacked that enthusiasm which he had been in the habit of communicating to the gentlemen behind him. I noticed, too, that during the course of one of his electoral campaigns this summer, at Sherbrooke, he may have thought it would be well before an audience so distinguished as that which faced him there, to put aside his fighting posture.
Anyway, we read in the news-10 p.m. papers, and it was placarded throughout the land, that this new and courageous leader had come down to the province of Quebec and freely admitted the paternity and his advocacy of the conscription measure and other measures of a similar nature. The trouble was that

the right hon. gentleman, having in mind the thoughts to which I have just alluded, forgot to make the remarks ascribed to him in the press throughout the country-the very remarks for which he received encomiums throughout the West and Ontario. It was freely stated, and it has never been contradicted, that in Sherbrooke the right hon. gentleman made no reference whatever to those matters.
However, I did not intend to go at length into the question of the career of the Prime Minister and of his fitness for the post which he now occupies. I intend tonight to discuss as briefly as I can the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and the consequence of that amendment-the dissolution of Parliament and an appeal to the people.
We have in the House three different schools of thought. We have a number of hon. gentlemen to my left, who believe that in all things and in all matters the members of this House should be the mouthpieces of their constituents, and that in all things and in all matters they should represent with the fidelity of a gramophone the views which at that moment find support in the local riding, altogether irrespective, I am sorry to say, of the general good and the general welfare of the people. The adoption of this theory would make of this House nothing but an assembly of delegates whose mandate would be revocable at will, and those who hold their positions would hold them only by a very precarious tenure, depending entirely upon whatever wind, for good or for evil, was blowing in the constituency.
To the hon. member from Red Deeer (Mr. Michael Clarke) I will say this: he has been for many years, and still is, I think, the guardian in this House of the Gladstonian traditions. He has too much respect for and too much knowledge of the British constitution to share with his colleagues the views which some of them have espoused.
There is another point of view, that held by a number of hon. gentlemen oposite. They adopt a point of view which I might call, although it may offend them, an American one. They take their principles from the American Constitution which states that a government, or a ministry, or a member, or a congressman is elected for a certain term of years and may remain in office for that full term. It is true, having regard for our Constitution and for proper parliamentary practice, they

hold that they depend for the length of time during which they might hold office, on their majority in the House of Commons-In our present political position and if we take into consideration almost every government which has been in power since Confederation, this would really mean nothing more nor less than that the Government could remain in power for their full term unless such purely accidental circumstances as death or appointments to lucrative offices under the Crown had so diminished the numbers of their supporters that they no longer had a majority in the House. In other words, hon. gentlemen opposite hold that their tie to office is to be assimilated to the marriage tie-only to be dissolved by death or the Senate.
There is another point of view, that held by those on this side of the House, who believe in and are followers of Liberal principles. We believe that whilst no temporary outburst of sectional feeling or passing breeze of popular fancy should affect, to the extent of requiring a dissolution, any government strong in the confidence of the saner elements of the population and recently come from the electorate, there is no doubt that a government, to remain in power, must have a steady, constant support from the majority of the people, and that such support must be inspired by the trust which the majority had in that government's programme as outlined before them in an election previously held. We contend that the dictum of Edmund Burke " that the value, spirit and essence of the House of Commons consists in its being the express image of the feeling of the nation " is the proper constitutional standpoint to take. We believe-and I do not think I shall be contradicted by any supporter of the Government-that this House of Commons is not the image of the people of this country; that it d<5es not represent the feelings of the nation; that it represents only a distorted view of the feelings of the nation, and further, that should this House of Commons be dissolved and we be returned before the people, there will be a great and material change in its personnel and composition.
May I glance for the moment at the history of this Government? It was formed, amidst the plaudits of the whole country, by what was said to be the best and most patriotic citizens of Canada, united for one purpose alone, to win the war. I do not wish to quote at any great length from the assertions of my hon. friends opposite, but it was repeated on the platform and in

the press that this was merely a temporary alliance, and that as soon as the ' war was over, the Unionist party would be dissolved into its constituent * parts.
I do not care to say much with regard to the means taken by hon. gentlemen opposite to win the election, except that, owing to their appeal, thousands and tens ol thousands of people throughout the country voted for the Unionist party and for the candidates thereof, people who, under other circumstances, have never had the slightest confidence in either. Having obtained power with a substantial majority, the Government proceeded to exercise this power with an autocracy which has seldom been surpassed in Canadian history. The most priceless, the most cherished rights of the people were trampled upon. Orders in Council were passed and put into force without consultation of Parliament and, in many cases, in direct violation of pledges made and given to the electorate. To every argument that right and justice were being violated and that public decency was being outraged, there was only one answer: "We must win the war.,'
No matter what took place, it was justified with that end in view.
As soon as the war was over, the reaction took place, and the people, who had, up to that time, been most submissive to authority were the first to demand with no uncertain voice that the privileges possessed by them and their ancestors should be returned to them. Though the administration has been growing steadily weaker and its majority in this House has been diminished at almost every division, it was considered wholly right, fair and just that the Government should carry on until such time as demobilization was complete. After demobilization was complete, when every newspaper of any standing in the community, when every man, outside of the House, of any standing admitted that the ministry of Sir Robert Borden and the Unionist party was doomed to an early end to its career, it was suddenly discovered that it might be well to form a new party and, with a new leader, to endeavour to re-establish the dwindling popularity of hon. gentlemen opposite. The new leader thus forced to take over the reins of power was faced with an onerous task. He had to reconstruct the cabinet and renovate the party. Had he been successful in accomplishing this we might have been justified in granting him our suffrages in order that he might retain power.
But what has he done? He has taken three new ministers into his Cabinet. One,
I am sorry to say, was not obliged to face the electors. Had it been otherwise, I am sure that the explanations which he would have given in answer to questions such as were suggested by my hon. friend from Brome would have been highly interesting to his electorate and to the country. The other two went before the people and were elected. These gentlemen are great personal friends of mine and I have no wish to offend them. I wish to congratulate them upon their appointment to office. But may I also say that I congratulate them on their peculiarly good fortune in representing such constituencies, and upon their still greater good fortune in being supporters of a party which could not~without extreme difficulty elect any one else.
Elections have been held in three other constituencies, seats traditionally Tory. In the one, the Government majority was reduced substantially, and in the other two the candidates of the Government met with ignominious defeat, with the result that there has been and is to-day throughout the country a very strong and almost unanimous demand for an election, which demand is joined in not only by the Liberals but by the most bigoted and fanatical supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite. On this question of the by-elections, may I quote a gentleman whose authority I am sure will not be questioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, the Rt. Hon. William Ewart Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone at one period of his career, whilst he was Prime Minister, suffered a number of losses in by-elections and we find that he-I am quoting from Gladstone's life-"laid before the Cabinet a pretty full outline of the case as to the *weakness of the Government since the crisis of last March and the increase of that weakness, especially of late, from the unfavourable character of the local indications." I submit that at the present moment in this country there is no doubt whatever about the unfavourable character of the local indications, the local indications being the by-elections held.
But there is something more. There is the unfavourable character of the local indications when we refer to the by-elections not held, when we refer to the badly needed reconstruction of the Cabinet, and the fact that it is impossible or almost impossible for the Government to have new ministers elected. We have heard a great deal of late about reconstruction, and I am reminded of the old homely proverb that in order to skin your rabbit, you must first catch him. Similarly, to reconstruct your

Cabinet, you must first elect your ministers. In studying the history of the British Constitution-and this history, when it is written, is to be found chiefly in the debates of the House of Commons-I find that a situation similar to that which exists here to-day existed in the Old Country not many years ago. In the year 1900 the Empire was engaged in a struggle in South Africa with the Boers. The struggle, though not one which would affect the integrity of the Empire, was sufficient to give cause for considerable uneasiness to the people of England. The English troops had met with some rather severe and unexpected defeats, and generally, the position was not of the happiest. In 1900 the Parliament was dissolved and the electors of England were called upon to elect a new Parliament. The Tory party, true to its principles and its best traditions, went to the country on one issue, and on one issue alone. They waved the flag. They alone were the patriots; others were the enemies of their country, and, as has happened before, the people of England, as were later on another and a better people, were deceived and the Tory party was elected. They dragged .on for some considerable time, until 1905, when we find that the peoplfc of England had become rather tired of this war ministry, and that the representatives of the people in the House were making exactly the same demand on the Government as we are to-day making on this Government! In that connection may I quote, because the circumstances are so similar, from Mr. Asquith? He said:
For let Us remember that when this House was elected in 1900, Lord Salisbury was the Prime Minister.
May I say that in 1900 when the Tory party came into power in England Lord Salisbury was the Prime Minister, but he was succeeded shortly afterwards hy the Rt. Hon. A. J. Balfour. So the circumstances were very similar to the situation here. The hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) was in power and he was succeeded by the present Prime Minister. To continue the quotation:
Where is the Ministry and where is the Party that Lord Salisbury left to his successor? The one, the Ministry, has disappeared. Nothing would have surprised the country more in the year 1900 than if they had been told that they were voting for installing on the Treasury Bench th'e gentlemen who at present occupy it.
May I say that nothing would have surprised the people of this country more
-rMr. Power]
than to have been told in 1917 that they were voting to install on the Treasury Bench the hon. gentlemen who now occupy it. He goes on:
' The Ministry has disappeared and! you have to look and search about for most, at any rate, of its more distinguished and experienced members in all sorts of unexpected quarters.
May I call the attention of the House to the fact that exactly the same condition obtains here. The most distinguished and most important members of the ministry are scattered in all sorts of unexpected quarters. Two of them now sit on this side of the House. One of them has even had his title to sit in this House challenged. Another of them has accepted a high position in the gift of the Crown, and still another, and I am sorry for him, has announced publicly that he will support his colleagues, and save them and keep them righteous and godly only when questions of international importance are being discussed. When these questions are not being discussed he leaves his friends to pursue their own course of salvation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought it was the other way.

My respect for the rules
of the House prevented my making the suggestion made by the hon. minister. To continue the quotation:
Where is the party? What has become of the party? The party, as every man 1 am addressing knows, has split and sundered beyond the salving power of any person.
With respect to the party which faced us after the election of 1917, we find a goodly number of the most respectable members sitting on this side of the House. Their independence and their courage have shown the way for them to come across the floor of the House and sit on the side where it is posible to be independent and to be honest in one's opinions on questions of public policy. I could go on quoting at considerable length, but since the hour is growing late I think it would be well to cut my remarks short.
Go on.

I could refer any hon. gentlemen who are interested in this matter and who wish to obtain constitutional precedents in regard to the question, to the Parliamentary Debates of the British House of Commons for February 1905, wherein they will find ample matter for discussion and for the enlightenment of their minds with reference to the true constitutional

view to be supported in this debate. But in order to show my impartiality and to prove that I am moved only by highest motives in supporting my hon. friend-
I will quote a gentleman whose authority may perhaps be more respected by hon. members oposite, and I will quote him in such a manner that I hardly think the advice which he gives will be ill received. The Rt. Hon. Arthur J. Balfour in February, 1895, referring to the Rosebery Ministry, which had at that time gotten itself into a situation somewhat similar to that of hon. gentlemen opposite, said:
I have never observed in the history of this country that any party of any Government have gained credit from hanging on to office, in the vulgar sense without power and with only the insignia of office, from hanging on to their places when they were deprived' of all real influence on the course of events and when the general trend of public opinion was against them. Under such circumstances the Government may possibly do good administrative work.
Possibly.
It may possibly continue to hold its tenure of office for one month, two months, six months, or even a year or more, but you will never find in the history of this country that this has had the result of increasing the credit of a Government with those on whose favour their fortunes ultimately rest.
You will see that this advice is given in the best interests of hon. gentlemen oposite. But if this were the only result, that their credit in the country would be diminished, I confess that we should not have very much ground for complaint. But by carrying on the course which they are pursuing, the very foundation of parliamentary government is being shaken, and the principles on which this constitution has been founded are being endangered. We then have the right to protest, as we do, in the most emphatic manner possible. I submit that it is useless for hon. gentlemen to carry on any longer. They have lost the confidence of the country. They have lost the confidence of every important body and every important interest in the community. The business community looks with horror on gentlemen who are able to lose $50,000,000 to $75,000,000 every year on the management of railways. Business men stand aghast at the probable cost of that new and useless ornament which we have added to the country's burden, namely, the Mercantile Marine. They are convinced * that it will not be many years before it will equal in deficits the other branch of the service, and that we
shall pay as much for it as for that other ill-fated adventure in public ownership.
With reference to the farming community,
I find it difficult to say anything more than what my hon. friends to my left can say. We know that the farmers have a good deal to say to the Government and the people of the country. With regard to the labouring classes, I have only this to say, that they too are convinced that hon. gentlemen opposite have not the confidence of the people. They are convinced that they are not properly represented by hand-picked gentlemen in another Chamber. They are convinced that if the Lords of the Council only go before the people labour will have that oportunity for which it has been waiting a long time.
Another class of the community about which we heard a great, deal in 1917, something in 1918, something in 1919, but a gradually diminishing amount as the years go on, have been the ex-soldiers, our boys at the front, our boys in the trenches, boys for whom the election was fought and, may I say, boys with whom some of the seats were won. These same boys have a word to say. May I quote from a manifesto issued by Mr. R. B. Maxwell in his official capacity as President of the Great War Veterans' Association, the largest body of organized soldiers in the Dominion of Canada?
Mr. Maxwell says:
Parliament has confessed inability to redeem former pledges and restore to returned soldiers and dependents in a substantial measure the economic advantages they would now enjoy but for war service. Parliament has shown reluctance to offset much "failure by general measures for the improvement of living conditions throughout the country whereby returned soldiers might more easily regain a secure foothold in the national life. Parliament now requires that those who served in the war shall share in the payment of the major portion of the war debt despite the fact that war accumulated wealth remains practically unmolested.
Parliament as at present constituted apparently cannot cope with distressing living conditions which affect not omy the returnen soldiers but the public generally. Parliament has denied to the electors of. Canada any opportunity since 1911 to assert their views upon domestic questions by means of the ballot. Parliament continues to ignore the fact that the demand for a general election does not arise solely from among returned soldiers hut is supported by the vast majority of those who have the interests of the country at heart and who view with alarm the increasing unrest. Parliament has outlived its mandate. The time has arrived for the people to declare themselves on the vital questions of the day. I therefore call upon you in defense of the basic principles upon which this association was founded to assemble in mass meeting with

your fellow citizens and secure without delay an unmistakeable expression of the wishes of the people in regard to the necessity of a general election.
Sir, we have heard the views of the authorized representative of the returned soldiers of Canada, those returned soldiers for whom we were prepared to do so much. I ask the hon. gentleman who said to the soldiers in France, "When you return Canada is yours," to only allow the returned soldiers a chance to vote in Canada -one little chance to exercise that franchise for which they fought. If you will only give them that little chance, if they are only permitted that opportunity, hon. gentlemen opposite will have earned their gratitude. They will have shown for the first time since they came into power that they are really prepared to agree to the wishes of the returned soldiers.
There is another class, and this class I mention last, because in my mind it is the most important. By means of a series of indignities and insults, without parallel even in the days of our earlier history, some hon. gentlemen opposite have alienated the sympathy of a whole province and of a whole race. In order to win victory at the polls a campaign of hate and a propaganda of detraction was launched, which I admit was to a large extent successful, and our province was pointed to as a pariah among the other provinces of Confederation. Experience has taught us that this enforced isolation has not affected us in the slightest degree, and we have not been annihilated or destroyed by the enmity of the central government. On the contrary, since we have been so splendidly isolated we have experienced our best and our most prosperous days. We find that the enmity of our opponents has united us and their offers of friendship will not divide us. It may be, Mr. Speaker, that one of our party has been detached from us, but the day and the hour of the electors of the county of St. Hyaeinthe-Rouville is at hand.
I have this much more to say with regard to that same province. We can forgive and we will do so. We will do so cheerfully as it is one of the precepts of the religion which most of us profess. But we will not forget, and we will never put it in the power of any Government to strike a blow at our prestige and our standing in the community such as has been attempted to be struck by hon. gentlemen opposite. Never again will it be possible for any Government, in order to win an election, to point to us as those Who have

wished to break the Confederation pact. Never again will the people of this country allow hon. gentlemen opposite or their successors to get into office by a campaign of calumny and of detraction such as has been waged. The people of the rest of the Dominion now know that in the province of Quebec there resides a population which is the sanest and most honourable in the whole Dominion, and that in spite of accusations of backwardness and of being priest-ridden, in no part of Canada are the citizens more free or more happy. We live in a province that is free and contented, but if I am to believe the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), the case is far different in our sister province. We are free, contented and happy and we have never been more so than since we have been forced into our splendid isolation.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have shown that the business community are with us with the exception perhaps of some who have been frightened by the voice of the Prime Minister and his satellites when they accused the leader of the Liberal party and his followers of Bolshevist tendencies. The Prime Minister by that accusation may have frightened some of the business community. But there are others, who realize that with the advent to power of members from this side of the House the day of the profiteer and of "special interests" is at an end. Those gentlemen and those interests will,
I am sure, support to their utmost capacity when any election is held, hon. gentlemen opposite.
I have shown that the labour classes are not supporting this Government. I have shown that the agricultural classes are not supporting this Government. I have shown that the returned soldiers far from supporting it are praying only for its dissolution; I have shown that through its own -fault this Government has earned the disdain and contempt of a whole race. Mr. Speaker, I submit that there is nothing further to be said on the question, that there is nobody left to support hon. gentlemen opposite, that they no longer represent and they no longer are the image of the people of this country. I would like in conclusion, if I may be permitted, to quote just two lines of poetry. It is not my habit to quote poetry, but this is so applicable to the situation that I feel I shall be doing a service by giving the quotation on the present occasion:
There is on earth a more auguster thing,
Veiled though it be, than Parliament or King.

And that, Sir, is the public conscience. On this occasion the public conscience has been outraged. The public conscience cries aloud for the hon. members opposite to resign; it cries aloud to this House to vote for the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King), an amendment which would involve a dissolution and would bring those hon. members before the bar of the public opinion of this country.
On the motion of Mr. A. Thompson (Yukon) the debate was ajourned.
